URL: https://koshinstudio.com/anime/axes/

# 6つの軸

  ガチアニメ診断が測っているのは、この6つ。
それぞれ2択で、どちら側に寄ったかが文字になります。

## 世界観 R / F

  舞台は、現実の延長か、別の世界か

  舞台となる世界が、いまの私たちの暮らしの延長にあるか、まったく別の理屈で動いているか。R（リアル）に寄る人は、学校や職場、家族のような地続きの場面で感情が動きます。F（ファンタジー）に寄る人は、魔法や異世界、架空の文明のように、現実を一度忘れさせてくれる設定ほど入り込めます。どちらが上ということはありません。

    R — リアル地に足のついた人間ドラマに心が動く

    F — ファンタジー現実を忘れられる別世界ほど燃える

## 後味・刺激 D / H

  観終わったあとに残ってほしいのは、重さか、爽やかさか

  物語の終わり方と、途中の刺激の強さに関する軸です。D（ダーク）は、容赦のない展開や重い余韻も含めて作品を味わえる人。H（ハッピー）は、苦しい場面があっても最後には報われてほしい人です。診断では、グロテスクな表現や恋愛といったジャンルの好みは別に聞いていて、この軸は「後味の好み」そのものを見ています。

    D — ダーク救いのない展開ほど記憶に残る

    H — ハッピー逆転と大団円で満たされたい

## 構成・テンポ C / S

  伏線を拾いたいのか、勢いに乗りたいのか

  物語の組み立て方の好みです。C（伏線・考察）は、序盤の小さな違和感が後半で回収される構成や、設定の謎を解く楽しさを重く見ます。S（テンポ・勢い）は、細かい理屈より、一話ごとの展開の速さと盛り上がりで引っ張ってほしい人。先を考えながら観るか、その場の勢いに乗るかの違いです。

    C — 伏線・考察伏線を拾って考察するのが楽しい

    S — テンポ・勢い勢いとテンポで一気に持っていかれたい

## サブテイスト P / A

  見せ場は、読み合いか、アクションか

  見せ場の種類の好みです。P（心理戦）は、言葉の裏の読み合いや、登場人物の駆け引きを楽しむ人。A（アクション）は、作画の見せ場や、迫力のある戦闘で気持ちが上がる人です。タイプコードでは、回答の平均がどちら側に寄ったかで、片方の文字が付きます。

    P — 心理戦読み合いと行間のドラマが好き

    A — アクション作画解放と迫力のバトルが好き

## 視覚・フェチ V / T

  作品を選ぶ決め手は、映像か、脚本か

  作品のどこに惹かれるかの軸です。V（映像美）は、色づかいや構図、演出のセンスそのものが入口になる人。T（ストーリー）は、絵が素朴でも、脚本が面白ければ追いかける人です。診断では、画質や年代の好みは別の項目として聞いていて、タイプコードには入れていません。

    V — 映像美映像と演出のセンスでハマる

    T — ストーリー脚本とストーリーの面白さで選ぶ

## 視聴スタイル M / L

  じっくり味わうのか、気軽に楽しむのか

  観かたの習慣の軸です。M（熟読・考察）は、一話ずつ噛み締め、観終わったあとに感想や考察まで読む人。L（サクッと）は、面白ければ一気に観て、次の作品へ移る人です。作品の重さではなく、観る側の姿勢を見ています。

    M — 熟読・考察一話ずつ噛み締めて、考察まで読み漁る

    L — サクッと面白ければ一気見して、次の作品へ

## 画質・年代の好みについて

  タイプコードには入らない項目として、「新しめ・高画質が好きか、年代は問わないか」も聞いています。同じタイプでも、この好みと、好き・苦手なジャンルの違いで、選ばれる作品は変わります。

  診断をはじめる（無料・1分） (https://koshinstudio.com/app/shindananime/)この診断について (https://koshinstudio.com/works/shindananime/)

  64タイプの一覧へ → (https://koshinstudio.com/anime/types/)


---

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/anime/guide/

# アニメ診断の選び方

  診断の結果が「当たる」かどうかは、
何を測っているかで決まります。

  アニメの診断は、たくさんあります。名前は似ていても、やっていることは、同じではありません。ここでは、診断を選ぶときに見るところと、答え方、結果の読み方を、ガチアニメ診断 (https://koshinstudio.com/works/shindananime/)を例に書きます。数字は、このサイトで実際に測ったものです。

## アニメ診断には、二つの種類がある

- タイプを当てる診断。質問に答えて、あなたの「アニメの好みのタイプ」や、キャラクターを出します。結果は、ほとんどの場合「分類」です。

- 作品をすすめる診断。好みから、見るべき作品を挙げます。結果は「作品の名前」です。

  ガチアニメ診断は、この両方を一度に出します。6つの軸でタイプ（例：RDCP-VM）を出して、そのうえで、データベースから、運命の1作と、次点の2作を選びます。

## おすすめのアニメ診断を選ぶときに、見る四つのこと

### 1. 何を測っているか、書いてあるか

  「あなたはこのタイプ」と言われても、何を基準にしたのか分からなければ、納得できません。ガチアニメ診断は、世界観・後味・構成・サブテイスト・視覚・視聴スタイルの6つの軸で測っています。軸ごとの意味は、6つの軸 (https://koshinstudio.com/anime/axes/)に書いてあります。

### 2. 結果の理由が、分かるか

  タイプコードの一文字ずつが、どの軸のどちら側に寄ったかを表しています。結果の画面には、軸ごとの寄り方と、作品の適合度（%）が出ます。この数字は、並び順と同じ物差しから作っています（「82%より80%が選ばれる」 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/match-percent/)に、その経緯を書きました）。

### 3. 何作の中から選んでいるか

  診断が実際に使う作品は、6,074 作です。もとは 16,177 件あって、レビューの言葉が少なく、軸を決める手がかりが足りない作品は、落としました。落とした基準と、残った作品の偏り（2000 年以降が 90.5%）は、データベースの記事 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anime-db/)に、数字で書いています。

### 4. 回答は、どこへ行くか

  ガチアニメ診断は、回答を、この端末の中だけで計算します。サーバーには送りません。診断のデータの扱いは、あつかい (https://koshinstudio.com/privacy/)に書いています。

## 答え方のコツ

- 直感で答える。悩んだ質問は、「どちらかといえば」で十分です。

- 「どちらでもない」を続けない。真ん中ばかりだと、軸の向きが決まらず、結果がぼやけます。

- まず 12 問、続きは気が向いたら。12 問（約 30 秒）で、タイプと運命の1作が出ます。続けて答えると、最大 50 問まで広がり、画質・年代や、恋愛・ホラー・異世界転生などの好みの要素も、加味して選び直します。

- 見た作品は「見た」を押す。次点の作品に、差し替わります。

- 放送年は、結果の画面で切り替えられる。「こだわらない」「2010 年以降」「2018 年以降」から選べます。

## 結果の読み方：タイプは安定、1作は揺れる

  12 問と 50 問で、結果がどれだけ変わるかを、作り物の回答者 1,000 人で測りました（診断を12問にしたら、結果はどこまで変わるのか (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/shindan12/)）。

- タイプは、短くても、だいたい合う。6 文字を 1 文字ずつ見ると、回答のブレが中くらいでも、9 割以上は、同じ側に落ちます。

- 運命の1作は、質問を足すたびに、揺れる。12 問で出た 1 作が、50 問でも 1 作目に来るのは、5〜8 人に 1 人です。6,000 作から 1 つを選ぶので、少しの入力の差で、順位が入れ替わります。

  タイプを知りたいだけなら、12 問で十分です。1 作の精度を上げたい人は、続きに進んでください。50 問のほうが、「本当の好み」に、約 1.7〜1.9 倍、近づきます。

## 診断で分かること、分からないこと

- 分かる：あなたの好みの傾向と、その傾向に近い作品。

- 分からない：その作品を、あなたが面白いと感じるか。診断が測っているのは、好みと作品の「近さ」です。

- 偏りがある：データベースは、新しい作品と、よく語られる作品に、寄っています。古い作品や、あまり語られない作品は、選ばれにくいです。

- 好みは変わる：今日の結果が、来年も同じとは限りません。

## よくある質問

### アニメ診断は無料ですか？何問ありますか？

  ガチアニメ診断は無料です。まず12問（約30秒）でタイプと運命の1作が出ます。続けて答えると、最大50問まで広がります。すべて選択式です。

### アニメ診断は当たりますか？

  「当たる」の意味によります。タイプは、12問でもだいたい合います（作り物の回答者で測ると、6文字を1文字ずつ見て、9割以上が同じ側に落ちました）。一方、運命の1作は、質問を足すたびに揺れます（12問で出た1作が、50問でも1作目に来るのは、5〜8人に1人）。診断が測っているのは、好みと作品の「近さ」で、面白いと感じるかどうかの保証ではありません。

### 回答や結果は、どこかに保存されますか？

  いいえ。回答は、この端末の中だけで計算していて、サーバーには送りません。

### 何度やっても、同じ結果になりますか？

  タイプは安定しやすいですが、運命の1作は、答え方や、放送年の切り替え、好きなジャンルの選び方で変わります。すでに見た作品は、「見た」を押すと、次点の作品に差し替わります。

### 古いアニメも選ばれますか？

  選ばれにくいです。診断が使う作品のデータベースは、2000年以降の作品が90.5%を占めていて、新しい作品とよく語られる作品に、偏っています。放送年は、結果の画面で、「こだわらない」「2010年以降」「2018年以降」から選べます。

  ガチアニメ診断をはじめる（無料・1分） (https://koshinstudio.com/app/shindananime/)この診断について (https://koshinstudio.com/works/shindananime/)

  続けて読む：6つの軸 (https://koshinstudio.com/anime/axes/) ／ 64タイプの一覧 (https://koshinstudio.com/anime/types/) ／ 診断ガイドの入り口 (https://koshinstudio.com/anime/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/about/

# About

  English version (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/)

  Koshin Studio は、なんでも、ひとりで挑戦する場所です。
作って、試して、書く。ゲームや診断アプリなど、作ったものと、作り方・検証の記録を、ここに残しています。

## このサイトでできること

- Works (https://koshinstudio.com/works/) — 作ったゲームやアプリ。遊び方や仕組みも紹介しています

- Notes (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/) — 作る途中で測ったこと、詰まったことの記録

- ガチアニメ診断ガイド (https://koshinstudio.com/anime/) — 64タイプと6つの軸の解説、タイプごとの近い作品

- アニメ診断の選び方 (https://koshinstudio.com/anime/guide/) — 診断の見分け方、答え方のコツ、結果の読み方

## 作り方

  だいたい一人で、手元で動かしながら作っています。設計から絵から音まで通しでやるので、直したいところがあれば、その場で直せます。

  釣り合いの調整には、測る手を必ず用意します。ゲームなら自動で何百回も遊ばせて、どこで詰まるかを数字で見る。勘で三回いじって確かめるより、ずっと速くて確かです。その過程は記録 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anago/)に残しています。

> 感覚は当たっていた。
でも、原因は思っていたところになかった。
  導入も登録も要らないこと。ブラウザで開いたらすぐ始まること。それだけは崩さないようにしています。

## 記事の書き方と、訂正について

  Notes (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/) の記事は、実際のコミット（作業の記録）と、実測の数字をもとに書いています。決めている方針は、三つです。

- 数字の出どころを書く。記事の終わりに、何の記録から書いたか、いつ測ったかを書いています。

- 確かめていないことは、確かめていない、と書く。原因が分からないままのこと、実機で確認していないことも、そのまま書いています。

- 間違いは、直して、直したと書く。あとから分かったことがあれば、記事に追記して、更新日を変えます（たとえば穴子の記事 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anago/)は、寸法を変えたあとの数字を、追記しました）。

  記事の間違いに気づいたら、下の連絡先から、知らせてください。

## 使っている道具

  これまでに手を動かして使ったもの。名前を並べるだけでなく、何に使ったかも書いています。

## つくる言葉

        JavaScript主力
        ゲームもサイトも、動くところは全部これ

        Python実務
        書体づくり、絵の変換、統計を取る道具

        Swift実務
        iOS のアプリ

        HTML / CSS主力
        枠組みに頼らず、手で書く

## ゲーム

        Matter.js主力
        物理演算。すし積むの土台

        Canvas 2D主力
        絵は画像を貼らず、毎回描く

        Web Audio実務
        音も合成して鳴らす

## サイト

        GSAP / ScrollTrigger主力
        立ち上がりとスクロール連動

        Lenis実務
        滑らかなスクロール

        SVG主力
        ロゴの字も自分で起こす

## 置き場所

        Cloudflare Pages主力
        このサイトの置き場所

        Cloudflare Workers実務
        すし積むの番付サーバー

        Cloudflare D1実務
        番付のデータベース

        Firebase実務
        アプリの裏側（Firestore / Functions / Storage）

## 道具

        Git / GitHub主力
        全部ここで管理する

        Playwright主力
        自動で遊ばせる・自動で見て回る

        fontTools実務
        書体を必要な字だけに削る

        Pillow実務
        絵を配る形に落とす

        Xcode実務
        iOS の開発

  枠組みは、必要になってから入れます。このサイトも、動きを厚くする段になって初めて GSAP を足しました。外の CDN には繋がず、使うものは自分のサーバーに置きます。速いし、向こうが落ちても影響を受けません。書体も、既製品をそのまま貼らずに、必要な字だけに削って積んでいます。ロゴの字は自分で起こしました。

# あつかい

  English version (https://koshinstudio.com/en/privacy/)

  預かるもの、預からないもの。
最終更新 2026年10月

## 預かるもの

  番付（ランキング）に載せたときだけ、入れた名前・得点を、こちらのサーバーに預かります。作品によって、これに少し足したものを預かります。

  「すし積む」では端末が作った番号とその一戦の手順も預かります。手順は、得点の辻褄を見るためのものです。「端末が作った番号」は、その端末の中でランダムに作られる文字列で、同じ人の記録をまとめるためだけに使います。誰かを特定するものではありません。

  「10秒ピッタリで止めろ！」では、名前と3回ぶんの誤差、載せた時刻だけです。端末の番号は作りません。その日ぶんの順位は日付が変わると流れます。

  「寝返り将棋」では、オンライン対戦を遊んだとき（と順位表を開いたとき）に、端末が作った番号、名前（既定は「名無し」）、レーティング、勝ち負けの数、一局ごとの手順と結果を預かります。順位表に、名前とレーティングが載ります。AI 対戦と、同じ端末での2人対戦では、何も預かりません。

  名前は自由に決められます。本名を入れる必要はありません。

## 預からないもの

  それ以外は何も集めません。会員登録も、個人を追いかける仕組みも入っていません。広告を表示することがあります（下の「広告について」を読んでください）。メールアドレスも、電話番号も、位置情報も、一切受け取っていません。

  ただし、このサイトを置いている Cloudflare の、アクセスの集計（Cloudflare Web Analytics）が動いています。ページが何回開かれたか、どのページがよく読まれているか、といった数を数えるためのもので、個人を追いかけたり、広告に使ったりはしていません。

## 端末の中だけに残るもの

  ハイスコア・自己ベスト・寿司図鑑・言葉の設定・音の設定は、その端末の中にだけ残ります。番付に載せなければ、外へは何も出ません。ブラウザの保存領域を消せば、いつでも消えます。

## 記事のコメント欄

  記事の終わりに、コメント欄を置く場合があります。「コメントを開く」を押したときだけ、コメントの仕組み（giscus。giscus.app）と GitHub に接続します。押さなければ、接続しません。

  コメントを書くには、GitHub のアカウントが要ります。書いたコメントは、GitHub の Discussions（このサイトのリポジトリ）に保存されて、誰でも読めます。名前（GitHub のユーザー名）も、一緒に表示されます。消したいときは、GitHub 上で、ご自身で削除できます。

## 預けたものを消したいとき

  番付に載せた記録を消したい場合は、載せた名前を添えて、About (https://koshinstudio.com/about/) にある連絡先までご連絡ください。確認のうえ削除します。

## 置き場所

  このサイトと番付のサーバーは Cloudflare 上で動いています。番付のデータは、「すし積む」は Cloudflare の D1（データベース）に、「10秒ピッタリで止めろ！」は Cloudflare の KV に保存されます。

## 広告について

  ゲームを他のサイト（ゲームポータル）に出しているときは、そのサイトの広告の仕組みが働くことがあります。その場合は、それぞれのサイトの方針に従います。

  このサイトは、Google AdSense で広告を表示します。Google を含む第三者配信事業者は、Cookie などを使って、このサイトや他のサイトへの過去のアクセス情報に基づいて広告を配信することがあります。表示される広告の内容やその仕組みは、Google の広告に関するポリシー (https://policies.google.com/technologies/ads?hl=ja)に説明があります。

  パーソナライズ広告は、Google の広告設定 (https://adssettings.google.com/)でいつでも無効にできます。第三者配信事業者の Cookie は、aboutads.info (https://www.aboutads.info/choices/) からも無効にできます。欧州経済領域（EEA）・英国からのアクセスでは、Google が用意する同意の画面が先に出ます。広告に使うこと以外の目的で、こちらが Cookie の情報を受け取ることはありません。

## 子どもについて

  年齢を尋ねていませんし、年齢に関わる情報も集めていません。番付に名前を載せる以外に、こちらへ届くものはありません。

## このページの更新と、お問い合わせ

  2026 年 10 月 17 日に、アフィリエイト（紹介リンク）の記述を外しました。現在、このサイトの記事には、紹介リンクはありません。今後、リンクを付けることがあれば、記事の冒頭と、このページに書きます。

  このページの内容についてのご質問は、About (https://koshinstudio.com/about/) にある連絡先までお願いします。

# Setting the rules of Negaeri Shogi by playing AI against AI: one change that worked, six that broke

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/negaeri-balance/)

  Development log of Negaeri Shogi / September 2026

  Negaeri Shogi (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/negaeri-shogi/) is a shogi-style game on a 6×6 board played a bit like Othello. Pieces you sandwich defect to your side and are promoted at the same time. If the new moves of a promoted piece create another sandwich, the flips continue. That is a chain.

  The rules come down to about ten numbers. I did not set them by feel. I ran dozens of AI-vs-AI games per candidate and measured. Only one change really worked; most of the others broke the game. I keep the ways they broke here.

  The numbers come from the measurement log in the game’s README (as of 13 September 2026). They are AI-vs-AI results. Balance between human players has not been verified enough yet.

## What I measured, and how

  The AI is a home-made alpha-beta search. I made depth-3 AIs play each other and counted:

- Share of drops that cause a flip. If low, most moves do nothing.

- Average game length. Too short means a one-sided game.

- First player’s win rate. Closer to 50% is fairer.

- Share of games with a chain of 3 or more. Chains are the point of the game.

- Lead changes. Too few: whoever is ahead early wins. Too many: it flips every move and feels random.

  Candidates were compared at 40 games each; final numbers use 100 games. Anyone can re-run it with the README commands (npm run report, npm run sweep).

## The first rules barely did anything

  At first a sandwich only worked along the directions a piece can move in shogi. In AI-vs-AI games, only 2% of drops caused a flip. Games lasted 16 moves and the first player won 71%. A flipping game where almost nothing flipped.

    Stage | Drops that flip | Avg. moves | First player wins

      Start (move directions only, empty board) | 2% | 16 | 71%

      All 8 directions | 8% | — | —

      Formation start position | — | 29 | —

      Pieces next to the king are safe | 42% | 51 | 33%

      One extra pawn in hand for the first player | 42% | 61 | 47%

      Board edge counts as the end of a sandwich | 81% | 53 | 59%

  The first player’s win rate jumps 71%, 33%, 47%, 59% because each rule change moved the advantage somewhere else. Every change needed a fresh measurement.

## The change that mattered: the edge is an anchor

  If a run of enemy pieces ends at the edge of the board, it counts as sandwiched. Pieces pushed against the edge defect together. This took flipping drops from 42% to 81%. Compared with other ideas at 40 games each:

    Idea | Flips per move | Games with a 3+ chain | Lead changes

      Before | 0.76 | 15% | 7.0

      Edge as anchor | 2.51 | 85% | 7.4

      + dropped piece is promoted too | 3.06 | 80% | 9.9

      Dropped piece promoted, alone | 0.72 | 13% | 5.0

      Chain limit of 3 | 0.71 | 8% | 5.8

      Piece-count result at 60 moves | 0.69 | 3% | 4.8

  Promoting the dropped piece too adds flips, but lead changes rise to 9.9 and the lead flips nearly every move, which thins out the shogi side of the game. I left it out (one setting turns it on).

## What I tried and dropped

    Idea | What happened

      Off-direction sandwiches reach only 1 square | Games with a 3+ chain fell from 95% to 13%. The reach of a sandwich was the engine of chains.

      5×5 board | Flips per move rose from 2.88 to 5.99, but the first player won 70%. Games were short (35 moves).

      Remove the king guard | Games ended in 17 moves on average and the first player won 95%. Guards defect at once and the king is left bare.

      Chain limit of 8 | Almost identical (2.86 vs 2.88 flips per move). The limit of 5 hardly mattered.

      Dropped piece promoted by a big flip | More flips, but 9.9 lead changes: it flips every move.

      Piece-count result at 60 moves | Games with a 3+ chain fell to 3%.

  The most useful row was “a limit of 8 changes nothing.” Raising the limit sounds like it should add chains. Measured, the result barely moved, so the limit of 5 was not doing much. I was about to tune a number that did not matter.

## Pieces next to your king never defect

  In this game a piece next to your own king does not defect. Removing that rule is the third row above: 17 moves on average and a 95% first-player win. Guards defected in a single move and the king was taken early. It is one plain sentence in the rules, and the game does not work without it.

## Current numbers (100 AI-vs-AI games, depth 3)

    Measure | Value

      Average length | 52.7 moves

      Board fill | 61%

      Drops that flip | 81%

      Flips per move | 3.08

      Games with a 3+ chain | 87%

      Games with a 4+ chain | 38%

      Average lead changes | 10.4

      Games with no lead change | 0%

      Games where the loser led at some point | 98%

      Point at which the result is decided | 81% of the way through

      First player’s win rate | 61%

  The board changes hands again and again and stays close to the end, yet it is not luck: a depth-3 AI beat a depth-2 AI in 20 of 24 games (as first or second player). 98% of games end by taking the king, so sandwiching stays a means and the shogi goal stays the goal.

## Still unsolved: the first player’s edge

  In the final measurement the first player won 61% (59% in an earlier, separate measurement). That is 11 points from 50%. I tried five handicap setups and found none clearly better.

    Handicap | First player wins

      None | 33%

      One extra pawn in the first player’s hand (current) | 61%

      One extra pawn on the first player’s side of the board | 38%

      Move one of the first player’s board pawns into hand | 64%

      Extra pawn in hand for the first player and extra pawn on the board for the second | 27%

  Pieces come in whole units, and the same “one pawn” is worth very different amounts depending on where it is placed: a point-symmetric addition moved the result by +5 points in one case and −34 in the other. Adding up small pieces cannot tune it to 50%.

  In online play, matchmaking gives the first move to the lower-rated player, which partly cancels the gap. That is not a fix. Games between humans are still to be checked.

## What I learned

> Half the changes that felt like good ideas broke the game when I measured them.

- Build the measuring tool first. Being able to run AI-vs-AI games automatically is what let me compare six ideas under the same conditions.

- Some numbers do nothing. The chain limit gave the same result at 5 and at 8.

- Ideas that break the point of the game only show up in measurement. “Reach one square” looked like it would restore each piece’s character; it cut chains from 95% to 13%.

- Say what is not fixed. The first-player gap is still 61%.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/negaeri-balance/). Numbers come from the README measurement log (13 September 2026). Negaeri Shogi (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/negaeri-shogi/) is free to play in the browser.

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Negaeri Shogi (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/negaeri-shogi/)

# ITMS-91064 “Invalid Binary”: NSPrivacyTracking was true but NSPrivacyTrackingDomains was empty

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/itms-91064/)

  Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  I uploaded my iOS app, Torecadash, and Apple's automated review rejected build 877 as an “Invalid Binary”. The error code was ITMS-91064. The cause was a combination of two entries in the privacy manifest (PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy). This is what happened and how I fixed it, written from my commit history.

## What happened

  Build 877 was rejected as an “Invalid Binary” by Apple's automated review (October 6, 2026). In other words, it was stopped by a machine check, before any human reviewer saw it.

## The cause: tracking declared, but the domain list was empty

  The privacy manifest had these two entries:

    Key | Value

    NSPrivacyTracking (whether the app tracks) | true

    NSPrivacyTrackingDomains (domains used for tracking) | an empty array

  Apple's check rejects this combination as a contradiction: the app declares that it tracks, but lists no domain at all.

  Should I have just set NSPrivacyTracking to false? No. The app shows AdMob ads (banner, native and app-open) and personalizes them for users who agreed to ATT (App Tracking Transparency). The app really does track, so true is the correct declaration. The thing to fix was the empty domain list.

## The fix: list the domains

  However, Google does not publish an official list of tracking domains for AdMob. So I added widely used ad-serving domains:

- googlesyndication.com

- googleadservices.com

- doubleclick.net

- google.com

  I confirmed that the Release configuration builds (xcodebuild reported BUILD SUCCEEDED).

## What I have not verified

  The commit only records that the build succeeds. At the time of writing, I have no record of whether Apple accepted the fixed build. I also could not check whether the domains above cover every domain AdMob uses for tracking, because there is no official list.

## What I learned

> A declaration and its contents can be cross-checked by a machine.

- If you declare that you do it, write the contents (the domains) too. One without the other is rejected as a contradiction.

- When rejected, don't escape by deleting the declaration. If the app really does it, keep the declaration true and fill in the contents.

- When there is no official list, write down how far you verified.

  This article was written from the commit record (October 6, 2026). It is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/itms-91064/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Negaeri Shogi

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/works/negaeri-shogi/)

  Sandwiched pieces defect to your side.
Defected pieces get promoted.

  Play now (https://koshinstudio.com/play/negaeri-shogi/)

  Free. Runs in your browser, no install or sign-up. The game is available in English and Japanese.

      The starting position

      Mid-game against the AI

## What it is

  A small 6×6 board and shogi pieces, played like Reversi: drop a piece from your hand so that it sandwiches your opponent’s pieces in a line, and the sandwiched pieces flip to your side. Every piece that flips is also promoted (pawn to tokin, rook to dragon, bishop to horse). A promoted piece moves in new ways, so it can create new sandwiches, and the flips chain. A single move can change the whole board.

## Rules in short

- Four kinds of pieces: king, pawn, rook and bishop. They move as in shogi.

- On your turn you either drop a piece from your hand (this is when sandwiching happens) or move a piece on the board (no flipping).

- Sandwiching works in all 8 directions. The edge of the board also counts as an end, so pieces pushed against the edge can flip together.

- Kings never flip. Pieces next to your own king do not flip either, so the squares around the king are safe.

- Capture the opponent’s king to win. If neither side can move, the player with more pieces wins.

- Online games have 3 minutes per player, plus 5 seconds per move.

## Ways to play

- Two players on one device.

- Against the AI at three levels (weak, medium, strong). The AI runs in your browser.

- Online against another player, with an Elo-style rating and a ranking. A name is stored, and no sign-up is needed.

## About the balance

  The numbers (how many pieces each side holds, the king’s protection) were tuned by AI self-play. Balance in human-versus-human games has not been verified yet. If one side feels too strong, please tell me.

  Play now (https://koshinstudio.com/play/negaeri-shogi/)

  This is the English version of the Japanese page (https://koshinstudio.com/works/negaeri-shogi/). Online play stores your name, rating and results (see the privacy page (https://koshinstudio.com/privacy/), in Japanese).

# Privacy

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/privacy/)

  What is stored and what is not.
Last updated October 2026

## What is stored

  Only when you submit to a ranking, the name and score you enter are stored on our servers. Some works store a little more, as described below.

  Sushi Stack also stores a number generated on your device and the move history of that run. The history is used to check that the score adds up. The device number is a random string created on your device and is used only to group records from the same device. It does not identify anyone.

  Stop at 10 seconds stores only your name, the errors of your three tries and the time you submitted. It does not create a device number. The day’s ranking is cleared when the date changes.

  Negaeri Shogi, when you play online (and when you open the ranking), stores a device-generated number, your name (default: “Anonymous” in Japanese), your rating, win/loss counts, and the moves and result of each game. Your name and rating appear in the ranking. Playing against the AI, or two players on the same device, stores nothing.

  Anime Type Quiz calculates your answers on your device only and sends them nowhere.

  You can choose any name. You do not need to use your real name.

## What is not stored

  Nothing else is collected. There is no registration and no mechanism to track individuals. We do not receive your email address, phone number or location.

  The site runs Cloudflare Web Analytics, which counts how many times pages are opened and which pages are read. It is not used to track individuals or for advertising.

## What stays only on your device

  High scores, personal bests, collection data, language and sound settings stay only on your device. If you do not submit to a ranking, nothing leaves your device. Clearing your browser’s storage removes it.

## Comments on articles

  Some articles have a comments section. Only when you press “Open comments” does your browser connect to giscus (giscus.app) and GitHub. If you do not press it, no connection is made. Writing a comment requires a GitHub account, and comments are public, stored in GitHub Discussions with your GitHub username. You can delete your own comment on GitHub.

## If you want something deleted

  To remove a record you submitted to a ranking, contact the address on the About page (https://koshinstudio.com/about/) (Japanese) with the name you used. We will confirm and delete it.

## Where it is hosted

  This site and the ranking servers run on Cloudflare. Sushi Stack and Negaeri Shogi rankings are stored in Cloudflare D1 (a database), and Stop at 10 seconds in Cloudflare KV.

## About advertising

  When our games are published on other sites (game portals), that site’s own advertising systems may apply, under that site’s policy.

  This site shows ads through Google AdSense. Google and other third-party vendors may use cookies to serve ads based on a user’s previous visits to this site or other sites. Details are in Google’s advertising policies (https://policies.google.com/technologies/ads).

  You can turn off personalized advertising at any time in Google Ad Settings (https://adssettings.google.com/), or opt out of third-party vendors’ cookies at aboutads.info (https://www.aboutads.info/choices/). Visitors in the European Economic Area and the UK first see a consent prompt provided by Google. We do not receive cookie information for any purpose other than ads.

## Children

  We do not ask for age and do not collect information related to age. Apart from the name you put in a ranking, nothing reaches us.

  This is the English version of the Japanese privacy page (https://koshinstudio.com/privacy/). If they differ, the Japanese page is the original.

# Anime Type Quiz

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/works/shindananime/)

  12 questions, 6 axes.
Your anime type, and the one anime that fits you right now.

  Start the quiz (free, about 1 minute) (https://koshinstudio.com/app/shindananime/en/)

  Free, runs in your browser, no sign-up. Your answers never leave your device.

## What it is

  The Anime Type Quiz is a free quiz that finds the anime that suits you right now. It asks up to 50 questions about six axes (world, aftertaste, structure, taste, visuals and viewing style), your taste in picture quality and era, and themes such as romance, gore and isekai. Twelve questions are enough to get your six-axis type; the rest are optional. From your answers it works out the direction of each axis and gives you a type code (for example RDCP-VM) and a nickname. There are 64 possible types.

  Unlike most personality quizzes, it does not stop at the type. It then picks, from a database of over 6,000 anime, the one closest to you at the moment.

## It picks real titles

  You get a “destined pick” and two runners-up. Even people with the same type get different titles, because the pick also takes into account the years you prefer and the themes you like or dislike. If you have already seen a title, press “Seen it” and the next best match moves up.

  Closeness between titles is measured by cosine similarity of the six-axis vectors. Popularity and era preferences add only a little, on purpose: if they counted for more, the same few titles would come up for everyone.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many questions, and how long does it take?

  Twelve questions (about 30 seconds) give you your type and your destined pick. If you keep going, up to 50 questions refine the result with era and theme preferences. Every question is multiple choice.

### Are my answers or results stored anywhere?

  No. Your answers are calculated on your device and are not sent anywhere.

### Will the same type always get the same anime?

  No. The pick also reflects the years you prefer and the themes you like or avoid, so it differs from person to person.

### Do I need to install anything?

  No. It works in any browser, on a phone or a computer.

### Where do the data and the English titles come from?

  The database is built from publicly available information about anime and is used only for per-title tendencies; it does not keep review text. English titles and detail links come from AniList. A few titles have no English title yet and show the original Japanese title. Streaming availability differs by country, so the buttons link to JustWatch and other services rather than to a single store.

  Start the quiz (free, about 1 minute) (https://koshinstudio.com/app/shindananime/en/)

# Toreca Dash (トレカダッシュ)

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/works/torecadash/)

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/works/torecadash/)

  Other languages: 日本語 (https://koshinstudio.com/works/torecadash/)

  Lotteries, pre-orders, first-come sales.
The Japanese card drops that are hard to keep up with, in one place, with alerts.

  Open in the App Store (https://apps.apple.com/jp/app/id6788758920)

  Free to download. Pro is an optional paid upgrade.

## What it is

  Sales of trading cards in Japan are announced one store at a time, on store sites and on X. By the time you notice, the deadline has passed. Toreca Dash collects announcements from stores and online shops across Japan and takes you straight to the page where you can apply or buy.

## Main features

### Feed

  See open lotteries, pre-orders and first-come sales, filtered by game and sale type.

### Alerts

  Get notified as soon as something new appears for a product or game you follow.

### Deadline calendar

  Lottery deadlines and result dates, day by day, so you do not miss an entry.

### Entry tracker

  Record the lotteries you entered, and the results and purchases.

### Map

  Share in-store stock and lottery information with other users.

## Supported games

  Pokémon Card Game, Yu-Gi-Oh!, ONE PIECE Card Game, Union Arena, Lorcana, Duel Masters, Dragon Ball, Gundam, Magic: The Gathering, Weiss Schwarz, Detective Conan, hololive, Digimon, Haikyu!! Babo-ca!!, Palworld (15 in total).

## Toreca Dash Pro (optional, paid)

- Unlimited product follows, keyword alerts and excluded keywords.

- The fastest alerts for first-come and surprise sales (the free version is about 15 minutes behind).

- Filter to stores near your location.

- Full notification history, entry statistics, calendar export and CSV export.

- Track the value and profit/loss of your collection from purchase records.

- No ads.

## Good to know before you use it

- Store information is mostly in Japanese. Store names, announcements and product names are shown as published in Japan.

- Many Japanese stores require a Japanese address, phone number or store membership to enter a lottery. Check the conditions on each store’s own page before you apply.

- The app shows the information and sends you to the store. It does not buy or enter lotteries for you.

- Screens are available in Japanese and English. More languages are being added.

## FAQ

### Is it free?

  Yes. The main features are free. Pro is an optional paid plan.

### Do I need an account?

  No. The feed, alerts and calendar work without signing in. Sign in with Apple is only used for map posts and the daily fortune.

### Is it an official app?

  No. It is an unofficial app made by an individual, and is not affiliated with any card game publisher or store. Information comes from stores’ public announcements; always confirm the latest details on the store’s official page before you apply or buy.

# Sushi Stack

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/works/sushitsumu/)

  Start with rice and merge matching toppings to grow them.
The final piece is the golden sushi tub.

  Play now (https://koshinstudio.com/play/sushitsumu/)

  Free. Runs in your browser, no install or sign-up. Available in 14 languages including English.

    On a computer, the score sits to the left of the tub and the ranking to the right

      Title screen

      Playing

      The sushi encyclopedia

    11tiers of toppings
    14languages
    300games verified by auto-play

## What it is

  You drop pieces of rice into a tub from above. When two of the same topping touch, they become the next topping up: rice becomes egg, egg becomes shrimp, shrimp becomes salmon, and so on, up 11 tiers.

  You lose when the tub overflows. It is that simple, but bigger toppings take more room, so stacking without thinking ahead gets you stuck quickly. Each time you choose where to drop, and it adds up.

  When a merge produces a topping that immediately merges again, that is a “chain.” Five in a row is a “big chain,” and the score jumps.

## What is in it

### The sushi encyclopedia

  You can see only the toppings you have made so far; the rest are shown as silhouettes. It is stored per device, so everyone fills it differently. There are 12 kinds in total (including gari, the pickled ginger).

### Ranking (online leaderboard)

  Today’s top and the all-time top. Enter a name and submit to be listed. On a computer, it is always shown at the right of the screen.

### The menu mode

  The chef calls out orders such as “two tuna,” and if you make exactly that within the time you get a bonus. The longer you keep fulfilling orders, the higher the multiplier, and it resets to one when you miss. Scores run about 1.6 times those of normal play, so it has its own ranking.

### Gari

  About once in twenty drops, gari comes instead of a topping. It removes one topping it touches, an escape for when you have stacked badly.

## What you need to play

  Just a browser. No install and no sign-up. On a phone, drag to choose the position and release to drop. On a computer, you can also play with the left and right arrow keys and the space bar.

  It supports 14 languages: Japanese, English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Italian, Polish, Turkish, Russian, Indonesian, Vietnamese, Korean and Chinese.

## How it is made

  The whole thing is one HTML file. It uses Matter.js (https://brm.io/matter-js/) for physics, and the sushi is drawn on a Canvas every time rather than shown as images. The ranking runs on Cloudflare Workers and D1, and the server re-verifies the sequence of moves it receives before ranking it.

  The balance was tuned by letting the game play itself and taking numbers first. That story is in the development log (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/anago/).

  Play now (https://koshinstudio.com/play/sushitsumu/)

# Stop at exactly 10 seconds!

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/works/stopwatch10/)

  Press start and count ten seconds in your head.
When you think it is time, stop.

  Play now (https://koshinstudio.com/play/stopwatch10/)

  Free. Runs in your browser, no install or sign-up. The screen text is in Japanese, but the game is just a start button and numbers.

      Before starting

      While counting. Nothing moves

      After three attempts

    3attempts per game
    3modes
    1,000one-thousandth of a second

## What it is

  The screen shows no numbers, no ticks and no sound. Between pressing and stopping, nothing moves. All you can rely on is the second hand inside you.

  You stop three times and see your error from the target. Some people are off by 0.5 seconds, and some stop within 0.02. It is shown per attempt rather than as a total, because that makes your skill easier to feel. The best single attempt of the three is also kept. The average is skill; the best single is luck of the day.

## Three modes

### 10 seconds, no hint

  The basic way to play: three attempts. There is no clue at all.

### 10 seconds, with a hint

  A clock is shown for the first 3 seconds only. Match your own beat to it and do the rest by yourself. The moment 3 seconds pass, the display disappears completely.

### 100 seconds, one shot

  One attempt only. While you count the 100 seconds there is nothing to do. If you leave the screen (switch tabs or the screen turns off), that attempt becomes invalid.

## Why three decimals

  Browser clocks differ in coarseness by device. performance.now() is deliberately made less precise as a Spectre countermeasure: Chrome in 5 µs steps, Safari and Firefox in 1 ms steps.

  If six decimals were shown, a device with a coarser clock would more often end in 000 and gain an advantage. In a game about being “exact,” the luck of your device would decide the ranking. So I cut at three decimals to put every device on the same ground.

## Nothing moving

  While building it, I once put a blinking lamp somewhere in the display. It became a stand-in metronome. If something flashes at 1 Hz in your sight, people can count along with it, and a game about counting by yourself vanishes entirely.

  Now there is nothing that moves periodically during measurement: no pulsing buttons, no blinking, no animation. From the moment you press until you stop, the screen is completely still.

## How it is made

  The whole thing is one HTML file with zero external libraries. The digits are drawn as SVG polygons in a seven-segment shape, so it depends on no font either. The sound effects use no audio files and are generated on the spot.

  The stop time is taken from event.timeStamp of pointerdown, because waiting for click adds extra delay. Your records stay in your device, per mode.

  Play now (https://koshinstudio.com/play/stopwatch10/)

  Development log for this game

- Making a 10-second stopwatch ranking fair: 3 decimals, ties and write counts (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/stopwatch-rank/)

  This is the English version of the Japanese page (https://koshinstudio.com/works/stopwatch10/).

# About

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/about/)

  Koshin Studio is a place for taking on anything, alone.
Make, try, write. Games, a quiz app and more, with records of how they were made and verified.

## What you can do here

- English hub (https://koshinstudio.com/en/) — games, tools and development logs in English

- Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/sushitsumu/), Negaeri Shogi (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/negaeri-shogi/), Stop at exactly 10 seconds! (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/stopwatch10/) — free browser games

- Hardcore Anime Type Diagnosis (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/) — an anime quiz with 64 types and 6 axes

- Gacha calculators (https://koshinstudio.com/en/calc/gacha/) — rate and pity calculators

## How I work

  Mostly alone, running things on my own machine as I go. Because I do everything from design to art to sound, I can fix what needs fixing on the spot.

  For balance, I always prepare a way to measure. For a game, I let it play itself hundreds of times and look at where it gets stuck in numbers. It is much faster and more reliable than tweaking by feel three times and checking. The process is in a development log (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/anago/).

> My feeling was right.
But the cause was not where I thought.
  No install and no sign-up. It starts right away when you open it in a browser. That is the one thing I try not to break.

## How the articles are written, and corrections

  The articles in the development logs are written from real commits (work records) and measured numbers. I follow three rules.

- I write where the numbers come from. At the end of an article I say which record it was written from and when it was measured.

- I write “not verified” when I have not verified. Causes I never found and things I did not confirm on a real device are written as they are.

- I fix mistakes, and say I fixed them. When I learn something later, I add it to the article and change the update date (for example, the conger eel article (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/anago/) got an addendum with the numbers after sizes changed).

  If you notice a mistake in an article, please tell me using the contact below.

## Tools I use

- Languages: JavaScript (the main one: games and the site), Python (fonts, image conversion, statistics tools), Swift (iOS apps), plain HTML and CSS written by hand.

- Games: Matter.js for physics, Canvas 2D for drawing every frame instead of using images, Web Audio for synthesized sound.

- The site: GSAP and ScrollTrigger, Lenis, and SVG (I even drew the logo letters myself).

- Hosting: Cloudflare Pages, Workers and D1 for this site and the ranking server, and Firebase for app backends.

- Tooling: Git and GitHub, Playwright (to let games play themselves and to walk the whole site), fontTools, Pillow and Xcode.

  I add a framework only when I need it. This site added GSAP only when it came to thickening the motion. It does not connect to outside CDNs; everything it uses is on my own server, which is fast and unaffected when others go down. Fonts are trimmed to the characters needed instead of pasting a stock font.

# App Store review sent “Guideline 2.1 Information Needed”: the six things Apple asked for

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/review-info-needed/)

  Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  I submitted my iOS app, Torecadash, to App Review for the first time on October 6 (4:24 a.m. Pacific time). What came back was not a rejection but an email saying “additional information is needed.” This is a summary of what Apple asked for.

  I do not write the review result in this article. I will add it once there is one.

## What arrived

  It was Guideline 2.1 “Information Needed — New App Submissions.” The reason given was that this developer account has little review history. Apple wanted more information so it could understand the app well enough to finish the review. It was not a finding that the app is defective.

## The six things requested

  I was asked to reply in App Store Connect and also to put the same content in the “App Review Information” notes field. The six items (summarized):

- A screen recording on a physical device. On a device with the latest OS, starting from launching the app, show the normal flow of use. If there are account registration, login and deletion, user-generated content (including the report and block mechanisms), or paid features, include those too.

- The purpose of the app and its intended users. What problem it solves and what value it provides.

- How to start using the main features. If login is required, the credentials or sample files.

- A list of the external services used. Data providers, authentication, payments, AI, and so on.

- Differences in features or content by region. If there are none, say that it works the same in every region.

- Proof of rights if the app deals with a highly regulated field or third-party protected material.

  The email also included a list of common problems: bugs and crashes on a real device, a demo account if login is required, screenshots that show actual use, submitting in-app purchase products together with the app, and so on.

## How it connects to what I fixed before

  The first item mentions account deletion and reporting user-generated content. These overlap with what I had fixed before submitting (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-review/) (Japanese). Account deletion removed map posts too and revoked the Sign in with Apple token. Posts had a banned-word check and a report-review queue. I had also already drafted the review notes: the main features work without login, where deletion is, reporting of posts, and what Pro includes.

  So the mechanisms existed, but I lacked something to show them. The screen recording in item 1 is exactly that.

## What I learned

> In a first review, you have to show the reviewer that it works.

- The recording on a physical device is explicitly required to start from launching the app.

- Put the same content in the notes field as in the reply. You can reuse it for the next submission.

- Before submitting, check that you can answer the six questions yourself. If the answers come quickly, you save one round trip with review.

  This article summarizes the email I received. It does not include the submission ID or other identifiers.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/review-info-needed/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Firebase 12 does not work with Xcode 15.2 (Swift 6.0 required): why I pinned Firebase 11.4.0 and AdMob 11.5.0

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/xcode152-sdk/)

  Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  I build my iOS app, Torecadash, on a 2017 Mac with Xcode 15.2. In this environment, newer versions of the Firebase iOS SDK and the AdMob (Google Mobile Ads) SDK do not build. This is which version breaks and which version I pinned, written from my hand-over notes (July 2026).

  The version numbers are as of July 2026. The situation may be different with the latest versions today.

## The environment

- Mac: MacBook Pro 13-inch (2017). macOS tops out at Ventura (13.7.8) and cannot go higher.

- Xcode: 15.2, the latest that runs on Ventura. It officially supports up to iOS 17.2.

- My iPhone runs iOS 26, so I cannot install onto the device from the local Xcode with a cable. The only way to test on the device is to build with Xcode Cloud and distribute through TestFlight.

- Locally I only check that xcodebuild compiles. SwiftUI previews almost never render on this Mac.

## Firebase: pinned to 11.4.0

  The newer the Firebase iOS SDK, the newer the Xcode it requires. My notes recorded this:

    Firebase version | What happens

    12.0.0 and later | Requires a Swift 6.0 toolchain (Xcode 16.2 or later)

    11.12.0 and later | Also requires Xcode 16.2

    11.5.0 onward | A bug in FirebaseDataEncoder.swift (Firebase issue #15029)

    11.4.0 | Confirmed to work reliably

  So I set the Swift Package Manager rule to Exact Version 11.4.0. Xcode keeps suggesting the latest version, and I do not follow it.

  One point is easy to get confused about. Xcode Cloud (the cloud build) runs the latest Xcode, but the pinned setting is kept as it is, so cloud builds succeed without trouble. If you pin to suit the old local Xcode, the same version also builds on the newer Xcode in the cloud.

## AdMob: pinned to 11.5.0

  For the same reason, I pinned the AdMob SDK (swift-package-manager-google-mobile-ads) to 11.5.0 (July 22, 2026).

- 11.6.0 and later: The SDK depends on Apple's MarketplaceKit, which requires Xcode 15.3 or later. On Xcode 15.2 the build fails at link time with Undefined symbols errors related to MarketplaceKit.

- A caveat for 11.5.0: This version does not yet have the new Swift-style class names (BannerView, RewardedAd, and so on). You have to use the old names with the GAD prefix (GADBannerView, GADRewardedAd, GADRequest, GADMobileAds, GADFullScreenContentDelegate, and so on).

  When I upgrade Xcode and raise the version later, I will need to rewrite the class names, not only change the version number. I left that in my notes.

## What I would tell someone in the same situation

- Pin with “Exact Version.” With an “up to next” rule, Xcode picks a newer version you cannot use.

- Write down “from which version it breaks,” with version numbers. A few months later, when you have forgotten why you pinned, the reason is still there.

- The limits of your local environment can be relaxed in the cloud. You can keep testing on a real device through Xcode Cloud and TestFlight even with an old Mac. (The free tier has a monthly limit, though. See builds not arriving in TestFlight (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-ci/), in Japanese.)

## What I have not verified

  The version numbers in this article come from my July 2026 notes. I have not checked what the Xcode 15.2 constraints look like with versions released since. The “breaks from this version” boundaries are the build results at that time.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/xcode152-sdk/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# iOS app freezes and is killed (0x8BADF00D): a SwiftUI computed property ran on every redraw

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-watchdog/)

  Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  For my iOS app, Torecadash, I received a report: “the app crashes a lot.” Reading the device log, I found that the app froze and was force-quit by the OS. The cause was that it recounted 951 articles every time the screen was redrawn. This is written from my commit history.

## What the log showed

  The hang log from the device had the exit code 0x8BADF00D and the line Failed to terminate gracefully after 5.0s. It means the OS (the watchdog) killed an app that did not respond within 5 seconds. The main thread was stuck in processing that went through NSKeyedArchiver. The device was also hot (Thermal State: serious), so work that normally finishes instantly took more than 5 seconds.

## The real cause

  What froze was the list of product articles in the “Following” tab, in a case with 951 articles.

  The article list (articles) was just a computed property. SwiftUI evaluates the view (body) many times, even when the article data has not changed. Each time, it redid four filters, a transformation and a sort over 951 articles on the main thread.

  Normally this finishes instantly, so you do not notice. Only when the device slows down from heat does it exceed 5 seconds and get killed.

## The fix

  I changed it to recompute on a background thread only when something actually changes: the article data, the receive mode, or the sort option. The result goes into a state for display (displayArticles, @State), so the main thread is no longer blocked.

  // (Illustration only. Not the actual code.)
// Before: every time body is evaluated
var articles: [Article] { fetched.filter…filter…map…sorted }

// After: compute in the background only on change, and keep the result
@State var displayArticles: [Article] = []
// recompute when fetchedArticles / receiveMode / sortOption change

## What I have not verified

  The only verification recorded in the commit is that xcodebuild succeeded (BUILD SUCCEEDED). There is no record that the freeze is gone on a real device. A hot device is hard to reproduce, so it is not easy to check. In this article I write “I identified the cause and changed the approach,” not “I fixed it.”

## What I learned

> Work that is instant on a normal day stops the app on a slow day.
  Computed properties are easy to write. But if you put one where it runs on every redraw, it gets slower in proportion to the amount of data. 951 items is not a small number. The obvious lesson, “decide where to put things by how often they are called,” came from a real device log.

  This article was written from the commit record (October 5, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-watchdog/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/u2028/

# Python splitlines() breaks JSONL: the culprit was U+2028, an invisible line separator

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/u2028/)

  Development log of the Anime Type Quiz / October 2026

  While building the data for the Anime Type Quiz (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/), I fixed a bug where the JSON broke. The cause was splitlines(), a perfectly ordinary function.

## What broke

  The quiz data comes from Filmarks and is stored in data/filmarks_works.jsonl. JSONL puts one JSON object per line, and you read it by splitting into lines and passing each one to json.loads. In Python I had first written:

  for line in path.read_text(encoding='utf-8').splitlines():
    r = json.loads(line)
  But when a synopsis contained U+2028 (LINE SEPARATOR), that line was split in the middle, and json.loads was handed JSON that ended inside a string, and failed.

## What U+2028 is

  U+2028 is a Unicode character meaning “line separator.” It looks almost like a newline. In JSON, it is valid to put it raw inside a string, and the writing side (json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False)) outputs it as is.

  The problem was on the reading side. Python’s str.splitlines() splits not only on \n but also on Unicode line boundaries such as U+2028. split('\n') splits only on \n.

  s = json.dumps({"a": "x\u2028y"}, ensure_ascii=False)
len(s.splitlines())   # 2  (one line splits in two)
len(s.split('\n'))    # 1
  Passing each half to json.loads raises Unterminated string. The short example above reproduces exactly that.

## The numbers in the real data

  I recounted both ways on the current data file.

    How it is split | Number of lines

    split('\n') (real newlines only) | 7,247

    splitlines() | 7,255

  The difference is 8. Counting U+2028 in the file gave exactly 8, in the lines of 2 works. Two works out of 7,247, under 0.03%, were enough to make the whole file unreadable.

## The fix

  One line:

  - for line in path.read_text(encoding='utf-8').splitlines():
+ for line in path.read_text(encoding='utf-8').split('\n'):
  I left the reason in a comment so that my future self would not be puzzled: when making JSONL, the only line separator is \n, so reading should split on \n only.

## Why it is hard to notice

- You cannot see it. Depending on the editor, U+2028 looks like a newline or a space. Staring at the synopsis will not find it.

- It is rare. 2 of 7,247 works. While you test with a small sample, it may never show up. It is the kind of bug that appears only once you have fetched everything.

- The writer is correct. Nothing written is wrong as JSON. What broke it was the reader’s assumption about what a “line” is.

## One more fix from the same day

  The same commit fixed another bug caused by characters that look alike but are different. When matching titles, Annict’s ＜物語＞ (full-width angle brackets) and Filmarks’s 〈物語〉 (Japanese angle brackets) did not match even though they were the same work. NFKC normalization turns the full-width ＜＞ into half-width, but 〈〉 stays as it is, so I removed both from the comparison string.

  Both are the same lesson: characters are not always what they look like.

## What I learned

> A function I used “for newlines” had a wider idea of newlines than I assumed.
  When reading JSONL, do not use splitlines(). Split on the character the writer used as the separator (\n), or use for line in f:, which splits only on \n. I am writing it here for the next time the data grows.

  The numbers in this article come from recounting the data file on October 7, 2026.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/u2028/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/torecadash-ci/

# No builds arriving in TestFlight: I had used up the 25 free Xcode Cloud hours (my first diagnosis was wrong)

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-ci/)

  Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  While developing my iOS app, Torecadash, I hit a bug: “new builds are not arriving in TestFlight.” The first cause I came up with was wrong. This is where I went wrong, how I noticed, and what the real cause was, written from the numbers in my hand-over notes and commits.

## The first diagnosis: “[ci skip] is the cause”

  On September 2, I got a report: “there have been no builds since 9/1.” My first diagnosis was that [ci skip] in my commit messages was stopping the builds. I had been adding it to documentation-only changes so they would not use up Xcode Cloud’s free tier (25 hours a month). Along with the diagnosis, I even wrote a rule: “do not use [ci skip].”

## The timeline did not fit

  Looking at Xcode Cloud in App Store Connect, it said:

> You have reached your usage limit. The limit resets on September 8, your renewal date.
  Usage over the last 30 days was 493 builds, 28 hours 14 minutes. The free tier is 25 hours a month, so it was used up.

  What showed my first diagnosis was wrong was the timeline. Only three commits carried [ci skip], all on September 2. The builds had stopped on September 1. The cause came after the effect, so it could not be the cause. Worse, the rule I made was counterproductive when the quota was short.

## Why did it run 493 times?

  The workflow’s start condition was “any file changed.” Counting commits over the last 30 days:

    Last 30 days | Count

    All commits | 1,146

    of which touched the iOS app | 219 (19%)

    Builds run by Xcode Cloud | 493 (3.4 minutes each on average)

  So 80% of the time, I was building the whole iOS app although only server code or documents had changed. On top of that, “Clean build” was checked, so every build skipped the cache and took as long as possible.

## The fix is a setting, not a marker

- Change the start condition to custom file and folder rules, limited to the iOS app folder and the Xcode project.

- Uncheck “Clean build.”

  My hand-over notes estimate this takes builds from 493 to about 94, and time from 28 hours to about 5.4 hours a month. That is a calculated estimate, not a measurement after the change.

## What I learned

> Check whether a cause explains the facts, using the timeline, before settling on it.
  My first diagnosis stopped at the first plausible cause. Something that happened after the effect cannot be its cause. This check takes a minute if done before announcing the diagnosis. In my hand-over notes (§183) I left a warning that “this diagnosis was wrong,” as a record.

  The numbers in this article come from my hand-over notes and the commit record (September 2, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-ci/).

  More in English

# Firebase Auth: force-quitting the app created anonymous accounts in bulk (waiting for currentUser to restore)

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/apple-signin/)

  Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  In my iOS app, Torecadash, a user reported: “once I kill the app, it asks me to sign in with Apple again.” When I looked, 17 of the 19 users were anonymous accounts that had been created and thrown away. The cause was how I checked, with a single line, right after launch. This is from my hand-over notes and the commit record (August 14, 2026).

## The symptom

  It only happened when the app was fully quit by swiping it away and then launched again. Leaving to the home screen and coming back did not trigger it.

## Looking at the real data

  I opened the Authentication user list in the Firebase console:

    Users | Count

    Total | 19

    Signed in with Apple | 2

    Throwaway anonymous accounts (created and last signed in on the same day) | 17

  Ten of the 17 were from August 13 alone. A new anonymous account was being created every time the app started again.

## Cause: reading something that had not been restored yet, synchronously

  Right after launch, the app checked Auth.auth().currentUser on the spot. If nobody was signed in, it created a new anonymous account.

  But as Firebase’s own documentation says, currentUser is not guaranteed to be restored from the Keychain yet right after launch. If restoration is late, it looks as if nobody is signed in. Then, just before the existing Apple sign-in state is restored, the app creates a new anonymous account. It is a race condition.

  The race only happens on a cold start. When the app returns from the background, Firebase is not initialized again, so it does not happen. That matches the report exactly.

## The fix

- Stop checking synchronously. The moment restoration is known to be finished is the first call of the state listener (addStateDidChangeListener). I made the decision only at that point.

- Add one safety net. At launch, the account-management side (AccountStore) now compares against the real server-side state with reload(), corrects any mismatch with its local record, and leaves a diagnostic log.

## One more thing I found

  During the investigation I learned that Sign in with Apple had never succeeded on a real device since I implemented it on August 7.

- The first error was that the sign-in provider configuration could not be found. The Apple provider had never been enabled in the Firebase console.

- After I enabled it, a new error said the credential was already linked. An attempt made before enabling had actually gone halfway through, and the Apple ID was already linked to this device’s anonymous account. The app showed this as an error, but in effect the user was signed in. I changed it to treat it as success.

## What I have not verified

  This is an iOS-side change, so I cannot confirm the effect on a real device until it reaches TestFlight. My notes say the top priority is to check that the Apple link survives repeated force-quits and relaunches. There is no result in the record at the time of writing.

## What I learned

> The state right after launch is not settled yet.

- “Not restored yet” is different from “none.” If you decide “none” without waiting, you create a new one.

- Symptoms show up in real data. Opening the console showed 17 throwaway accounts. I would have had a hard time finding this by reproducing “the sign-in disappears” on my own device.

- “Never succeeded” shows up as a missing success record. The clue was that none of the registered accounts had any Apple information.

  This article summarizes my hand-over notes and the commit record (August 14, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/apple-signin/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# A canvas becomes twice as large on Retina: inset:0 does not stretch it (a bug in a logo that bursts when you tap it)

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/logo-pop/)

  Development log of Koshin Studio / October 2026

  The top of this site has a large logo. When you tap a letter, it pops and particles scatter. After I rebuilt the logo with my own typeface, I was told “the particles come out of a strange place, not from the letter” and “it is still shifted to the right.” It took three stages to fix. Here are the cause and how I found it, with measured numbers.

## Rebuilding the logo with my own typeface

  The old logo was set in Latin letters built on a Mincho skeleton. I replaced it with my own typeface, Koshin Pop (rounded Latin letterforms drawn from scratch). The font is under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, which allows use in a logo.

  I extract the outlines of the nine letters K O S H I N T U D from the font file and turn them into SVG paths (tools/logotype_pop.py). The logo is delivered as a picture, so the site does not ship the font file. The font has several shapes for the same letter (base, pop1, pop2), so I lined up three combinations and picked the one with the best rhythm.

## Stage 1: after a tap, the letter did not return to its place

  I recorded positions over time after a tap. The letters did not return to where they started.

    Letter | Center before | 2 s after

    K (top left) | (327, 306) | (320, 313)

    S (bottom left) | (331, 442) | (323, 435)

  That is about 7 px off. A matrix(1, 0, 0, 1, -46, -42) was left over: the scale was back to 1 but the position offset stayed.

  Cause: the animation library (GSAP) rewrote the position that was already set on the letter’s SVG <g> (transform="translate(x,0)") using its own calculation, and part of that correction remained afterward.

  Fix: I split the element into a layer that holds the position (outer <g transform>) and a layer that moves (inner <g class="ks-ch">), and switched the motion to the browser’s Web Animations (when it ends, the effect disappears and the original state returns). I checked all 12 letters: the centers did not move, and the transform after the animation went back to none.

## Stage 2: “it is still to the right”

  After that fix I was still told the animation sat to the right. My measurement said particles started within 2 to 13 px of the letter’s center. What I measured and what was seen disagreed.

  I had measured on a 1x display, counting particle positions in screen coordinates. When I measured on 2x (Retina) and 3x (phone) displays, the CSS size of the particle canvas (#burst) was wrong.

    Display | Viewport width | Canvas width (before) | (after)

    1280 px, 1x | 1280 | 1280 | 1280

    1440 px, 2x | 1440 | 2880 | 1440

    390 px, 3x (phone) | 390 | 780 | 390

  Cause: I positioned the canvas with inset:0 in CSS, but a replaced element such as a canvas does not stretch to fill with inset:0 alone. It keeps its intrinsic size (its pixel count). On a 2x display the pixel count is doubled, so the CSS size doubled too, and particles appeared at twice the coordinates (toward the lower right). On a 1x display the sizes are equal, so you cannot notice.

  Fix: set width and height to 100% explicitly. After the fix, the canvas matched the viewport on every pixel ratio.

## Stage 3: emit from the letter itself

  Finally I was asked whether particles could come from the letter itself. Until then they came from the center of the letter’s box, so for a letter with an empty middle like “O” they seemed to come from nowhere.

  I now pick points along the outline of the letter’s path (getPointAtLength), take their on-screen positions, and send particles outward from the letter’s center with some scatter. The bottom row is drawn as “letter = mask”, so I look up the path inside the mask that the rect refers to. In the captures, “O” emits from around its ring and “U” along its shape.

## What I learned

> When measured numbers and what people see disagree, suspect the conditions of the measurement.

- The viewer’s screen is not yours. I measured only on a 1x display and judged “the offset is small.” On a 2x display the particles came out at twice the position.

- Measure in the space people look at. I counted logical coordinates, so the on-screen offset was never visible to me.

- Measure the state after an animation ends, too. That letters did not return was invisible while I only watched the motion.

- Keep position and motion on different layers. If one element holds both, one overwrites the other.

  The numbers come from operating this site’s top page in a real browser (Chrome) on October 8, 2026. I have not confirmed the fix on an actual Retina device; I reproduced 2x and 3x pixel ratios with browser settings.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/logo-pop/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# I counted “duplicates are practically zero,” but the audit reported 112 pairs

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/dup-zero/)

  Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  My iOS app Torecadash has a job that merges “duplicates,” where one product is registered as several products, every night. One day I counted by myself and recorded “duplicates are practically zero.” But the repository audit reported 112 pairs. My way of measuring was wrong. This is the story from my commit record.

  This is a development log of the app.

## I counted zero, and 112 pairs appeared

  Looking at the 112 pairs, for example one trading-card booster pack was registered split into 7 entries, even though the merge job was supposed to run every night.

## Cause: it timed out partway through, every night

  Running the merge over all genres takes about 15 minutes. But the time budget I had given the nightly scheduled run was 480 seconds (8 minutes). The order always starts from the same genre (Pokémon). So every night it timed out in the middle of Pokémon, and the later genres were never reached.

  My count was “zero” because only the range I was looking at (the first genre) was clean.

## The fix

- Rotate. Start from the genre after where the last run stopped, and stop when the time budget (6 minutes) is used up. The next night continues from where it stopped.

- First, run it to completion by hand. Running all genres to the end by hand took duplicates from 112 pairs to 0 and products from 2,753 to 2,570.

## What I already knew: one pass is not enough

  Two days earlier (September 5), I had learned something else about merging. When A is merged into B, B’s name can become the same as another C. Then one pass is not enough. In real data:

    Pass | Merged | Result

    1st | 138 | 53 new same-name pairs appeared

    2nd | 54 | 0 same-name duplicates

  Products went from 2,935 to 2,713. So the daily slot now repeats until nothing is merged (up to 3 times). This “timeout” problem sat even before that repetition.

## Three more things the same day

- Six open lotteries had disappeared because of another product’s list price. A 7,200 yen lottery (the official 360 yen × 20 packs) had been compared with another product’s list price of 27,500 yen left on the article and rejected by price. I added a condition: “fix only when it can be proven.” Across all real data, 10 matched the condition and all were sales at a normal price. I restored 11 to visible.

- False alarms in matching. Of 17 “article exists but hidden,” 9 had a replacement article visible under a different spelling of the same shop (like two different kanji spellings of the same store name). If the replacement is visible, it now counts as covered, which moved coverage from 87% to 90% and hidden items from 17 to 4.

- The audit itself had stopped. The reader part for audits misread a regular expression right after => as a division, and four audits were failing with ReferenceError. I changed it so that names it could not cut out are reported with a reason instead of being skipped silently.

## What I learned

> When you count “zero,” first doubt what you counted.

- The range you looked at is not necessarily everything. Only the first genre was processed every night, so counting only the first genre looks clean.

- For time-limited jobs, check whether it finished. Running and reaching the end are different.

- The tool that counts also breaks. When an audit has stopped, the result looks like “0 items.” You need a way to notice that it stopped.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 5 and 7, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/dup-zero/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# “It should shrink” was wrong twice: cutting AI calls and what I measured afterward

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-ai/)

  Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  My iOS app Torecadash collects information on reservations, lotteries and first-come sales of trading cards (Pokémon, Yu-Gi-Oh!, One Piece) and notifies users. It uses an AI (Gemini) to decide “which product an article is about.” While trying to reduce calls to that AI, things I had written down as “it should shrink” were wrong twice. In order, with the numbers left in my commits:

  This is a development log of the app.

## What I ask the AI

  The article title (for example “30th CELEBRATION Premium Deck Set Espeon”) is matched against a list of recent product candidates (the latest 60), and the AI answers which product it is. One call is about 3,083 tokens, of which about 1,800 were the same fixed instruction text every time.

## First: if the title is exactly a product name, no need to ask

  If a title matches a known product name exactly, there is no need to ask the AI. When I added this “short circuit,” 43% of X monitoring matched in real data. There were 0 disagreements (the short circuit’s answer differing from the AI’s). So I recorded that it should cut about 45%.

  But 90 minutes after deployment, the short circuit had not fired even once. Recounting, it looked like this:

    Source | Could short-circuit | Already free before | Newly saved

    X monitoring | 813 | 768 | 45 (2%)

    Others | 419 | 188 | 231 (32%)

  Before this step, there was an already free path that checks against the official catalog. Most articles that could be short-circuited were already settled there. Adding up what is newly saved, it is about 39 calls a day, about 4.5% of the total. Not 45%, but 4.5%.

> The share a rule applies to and the calls it actually removes are different things.
  If there is a free path before it, you have to count the difference. That is what the lessons field in my commit says. The logic itself was correct and safe, so I kept it. But as an AI reduction, it was small.

## Second: ask in batches

  The next main idea was to combine several articles into one call, because the fixed instruction text is then paid only once. Articles of the same genre share “the latest 60,” so the merged candidate list barely grows.

  In the design I took care of two things.

- Do not add waiting time. In measurement, a short window of a few hundred milliseconds could not batch anything (only 12 times in 24 hours did articles arrive in the same second). But waiting a few minutes would slow X monitoring’s rounds by 5 times. So I chose to “send the moment every still-running article has come to wait.” The safety cap is 20 seconds.

- Do not lose accuracy. When batched, the candidate list becomes the union for everyone, so an article can see other articles’ candidates. So the answer is returned as a real product ID, and I always verify that it is among that article’s own candidates. If not, I do not accept it. For an article with a missing reply, I ask again for that one alone.

  I measured the effect by reconstructing candidate lists from the real articles of the last two days (characters sent).

    Batch size | One by one | Batched | Reduction

    2 | 21,762 | 13,427 | −38%

    3 | 32,673 | 14,964 | −54%

    4 | 43,571 | 16,192 | −63%

    6 | 65,000 | 17,729 | −73%

## Third: deployed, and it never batched once

  Six hours after deployment, there were 47 product-matching calls and 0 batches. Although 2 to 7 calls came in the same minute, each was asked one at a time.

  The cause was the “send condition.” I had checked “number waiting ≥ number of unfinished jobs (pending),” but jobs that had come to wait were also counted in pending. X monitoring runs 32 accounts at once. If 31 had already finished, pending was 1. The moment the last one came to wait, the condition held and it was sent immediately as a single item.

  The fix was to check “are there zero jobs that have not even come to wait yet.” When the number completely finished plus the number now waiting reaches the total, send. I also shortened the safety cap from 20 seconds to 6 seconds. If only one item comes, waiting 20 seconds every time would be longer than one X monitoring run (17.8 seconds measured) and delay the rounds.

  During this check, the first short circuit was also reviewed. In 6 hours, 28 of 47 calls (60%) were handled without calling the AI. The short circuit was working correctly.

## What I learned

- Do not write the “share it applies to” as the amount saved. If there is a free path before it, only the difference is saved.

- Deploying does not mean it ran. “0 batches” was found because I recounted. If I had decided in advance that a log should say “batched,” I would have noticed sooner.

- The three numbers (4.5%, −38 to 73%, 60%) are all not what I first estimated. They are numbers re-measured on real data after deployment.

  The numbers in this article come from my commit record (September 4 and 5, 2026). I do not write amounts of money.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-ai/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)
