# Making a 10-second stopwatch ranking fair: 3 decimals, ties and write counts

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/stopwatch-rank/)

  Development log of the 10-second stopwatch / October 2026

  Stop at exactly 10 seconds! (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/) is a game where you count ten seconds in your head and stop. It is three rounds and the smaller your error, the better. When I added a ranking to it, I had to decide “what is fair” in three places. This is written from the README and code comments in the repository.

## Display down to three decimals

  Error is measured with the browser’s performance.now(). According to the README, this clock is deliberately made less precise as a security measure (Spectre). Chrome is in 5-microsecond steps, Safari and Firefox in 1 millisecond.

  What would happen if error were shown to 6 decimal places? A device with a coarser clock more easily ends in 000 and gets an advantage. The README’s guess is that iPhones would take the top ranks. So I decided to cut to 3 decimals and align all devices. For the start of measurement, I use event.timeStamp of pointerdown rather than click, because click adds extra delay.

## Ties happen more than you think

  With 3 decimals, an exact 0.000 comes up with probability 1/1000 per attempt. The chance that any one of three attempts is 0.000 is about 1/333. If you build a “best of three” board, ties at 0.000 will pile up.

  So for a tie, the one with the smaller total error in the other two attempts ranks higher. If that is equal too, whoever submitted first. Someone who hit 0.000 and also did well on the other two ranks above, so they can be told apart from someone with one lucky attempt.

  The “total” and “average” rankings have exactly the same order (it is just division by 3), so they are one board. Separately I placed a “best single attempt” board. The idea is that the average is skill and the best single is luck.

## Counting writes

  The ranking is built on Cloudflare Workers and KV (a key-value store). According to the code comments, KV writes are 1,000 a day on the free tier. To stay within that, I decided the following.

- The board for each mode is stored under one key. One submission writes at most twice (today’s and all-time).

- Submissions that do not make the ranking, and submissions with the same name that are worse than before, are not written at all.

- Only one row is kept per name. One person cannot fill the board.

  Also, since scores are reported by the client, cheating cannot be prevented. The README says so. So I operate on the assumption that it is reset every day. Days are cut in Japan time, and today’s board disappears in 3 days.

## What I fixed around the launch

- The range of accepted error. I accept up to the slowest result the screen can show (99.999 seconds in 10-second mode). Even terrible results are accepted, since they will not stay on the board anyway.

- Do not cache the read before a write. If KV reads have a short cache, a new value is written over a stale one and submissions that came in between disappear. Only the read before a write has no cache. View-only reads stay cached.

- Retry when it could not connect. At first, if the game could not reach the ranking when it opened, it did not show the ranking box and never tried again. Even if the ranking backend came up while playing, there was no way back. When three attempts are done and the box is still hidden, it now reads once more.

- Stay quiet. Until it connects, the ranking box is not shown at all and there is no apology message. I decided that being silent is better than showing an empty box or red text.

## A stumble on launch day

  When I first deployed to Cloudflare Pages, I did not pass --branch. The name of the working branch I happened to be on was registered as the production branch of Pages. After that, deploying with --branch main only went to a preview, and the public URL did not change. I did not notice for an hour.

  I fixed the production branch to main in the dashboard. One more thing I had confused: the branch name shown on the “Production” row of the deployment list is the name at the time that deployment was made and is not rewritten when you change the setting. To see the setting, look at the “Production branch” column in the project list.

## What I learned

> Fairness is made of digits, ties and write counts.
  None of them looks like what makes a game fun. But cutting to three decimals and deciding tie-breaking in advance directly affect how convincing the ranking feels to players.

  This article is written from the repository’s README, code comments and the commit record (September 8 to 12, 2026). The clock precision per browser is as stated in the README.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/stopwatch-rank/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# From 16,177 titles to 6,091: how the anime quiz database was built by dropping over 60%

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anime-db/)

  Development log of the Anime Type Diagnosis / October 2026

  The Hardcore Anime Type Diagnosis (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/) picks your “one anime of fate” from a database of more than 6,000 titles. Where did these 6,000 come from, and how were they narrowed down? This is how the quiz’s data was built, from the repository’s commits and the current real numbers.

## Three sources

- The title list of Annict (an anime tracking service): 15,971 entries.

- Anime on Filmarks (a movie and anime review service): 7,247 entries.

- My own list of classics: about 500 titles.

  The same title is merged into one. After merging there are 16,177 entries. From these I keep only what is usable for the quiz.

## The criterion for keeping: “clues to place it on the axes”

  The quiz describes each title on 6 axes (worldview, aftertaste, structure, subtaste, visuals, viewing style) and picks by closeness to your answers. So each title needs enough “clues to place it on the axes.”

  The clues are estimated from the number of words that appear in reviews (the review text itself is not kept; only the number of words is counted). Disparaging phrasing and negations such as “the animation collapsed” or “I did not cry” are not counted. A phrase like “god-tier animation” is not double counted. This “richness of clues” is given as a number from 0 to 1, and titles below 0.25 are dropped.

  Also, by default I exclude continuations of TV series and spin-off theatrical films (such as Doraemon or Conan movies). Standalone original films are kept.

     | Count | Share

    Titles after merging | 16,177 | 100%

    Dropped for too few clues | 10,086 | 62.3%

    Kept (the database) | 6,091 | 37.7%

  More than 60% of titles were dropped because they lacked clues. The quiz also does not use titles whose values on every axis are close to neutral (absolute value 0.15 or less). That removes 17 more, so the quiz actually uses 6,074 titles.

## What the remaining 6,091 look like

  The data was made on September 25, 2026, and I counted it again on October 8.

    Source | Titles

    Listed on both Annict and Filmarks | 4,354

    Filmarks only | 1,077

    Annict only | 619

    My classics list only | 41

    Richness of clues | Titles | Share

    0.8 or more (plenty) | 3,388 | 55.6%

    0.6 to 0.8 | 639 | 10.5%

    0.4 to 0.6 | 1,148 | 18.8%

    0.25 to 0.4 (barely) | 916 | 15.0%

  The median richness is 0.92. But 15% passed only barely. The axis values for these titles are less certain than for the others.

    Decade of broadcast | Titles

    2020s | 2,591

    2010s | 1,996

    2000s | 926

    1990s | 291

    1980s | 166

    1970s | 83

    1960s | 20

  Titles from 2000 onward make up 90.5%. I think older titles tend to have fewer words in reviews and find it harder to meet the criterion (this is a guess, not confirmed). Titles with an image number 5,632 (92.5%).

## Weak points of this method

- It is biased toward new and much-discussed titles. The more words in reviews, the more likely a title stays. Older titles and those rarely discussed are likely to drop. The quiz has a decade question that decides how much to downweight older titles, but the pool itself already leans toward newer ones.

- The number of clues is “how much was said,” not “taste.” Estimating 6 axes from word counts is a rough approximation.

- The data is as of when it was made. New titles have to be added every season.

## What I learned

> Most of the “6,000 titles” turned out to be “what was left of 16,000 after keeping those with clues.”
  It is tempting to say “covers all anime,” but in fact more than 60% were dropped for lack of clues. I think writing down how many I dropped and the criterion for keeping is what makes the quiz honest.

  The numbers in this article come from the quiz’s data (made on September 25, 2026 and recounted on October 8). Titles, review contents and rating scores are not included.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anime-db/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/match-percent/

# “80% was chosen over 82%”: the quiz’s match percentage disagreed with its ranking

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/match-percent/)

  Development log of the Anime Type Diagnosis / October 2026

  At the end, the Hardcore Anime Type Diagnosis (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/) shows “the one anime of fate” and two runners-up. Each has a number like “match 82%.” At one point this number disagreed with the ranking: “a title at 80% was chosen over a title at 82%.” I have re-measured how large the disagreement was, and I am writing it down.

## The number and the ranking used different yardsticks

  The quiz measures taste on 6 axes and computes a “closeness” (cosine similarity) for each title. But the final order is not decided by closeness alone. It is ordered by closeness × 0.82 plus the title’s rating (stars), popularity, era and taste elements (total).

  However, the match percentage on screen was built from closeness alone. The order was by the total and the display by closeness: two yardsticks. A title could rank first by total but have a lower closeness than second place. Then the screen showed “1st 80%, 2nd 82%.”

## The fix

  I changed it so the percentage comes from the same total as the order (September 25, 2026). The same day I fixed another contradiction in the display. Even when an axis bar’s value was exactly 0, it showed “leans X 50%.” It said it leaned when it did not. I made the minimum 51%.

## How big was the disagreement? Measure it

  The commit of the time does not keep the proportion. So I measured with the same 1,000 synthetic respondents (answering all 50 questions) as in the 12-question article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/shindan12/) (in Japanese). For the top 3 titles, I compare how the screen display would look in three ways.

- Old: integer % computed from closeness.

- Middle: integer % computed from total.

- Now: % to one decimal place computed from total.

  I counted two things. “Reversal” is when the 1st place % is lower than the 2nd or 3rd place %. “Tie” is when 1st and 2nd look like the same %. Answer noise is small (0.3), medium (0.5) and large (0.8).

    Display | Answer noise | Reversal | 1st and 2nd tied

    Old (closeness, integer) | Small | 40.3% | 14.1%

    Medium | 37.7% | 15.3%

    Large | 35.1% | 15.3%

    Middle (total, integer) | Small | 0.0% | 31.7%

    Medium | 0.0% | 30.1%

    Large | 0.0% | 27.7%

    Now (total, one decimal) | Small | 0.0% | 3.6%

    Medium | 0.0% | 3.9%

    Large | 0.0% | 3.8%

  With the old display, the top three were shown in reversed order for 35 to 40% of respondents. By this calculation about 2 in 5 people saw “the chosen first place is lower than the runner-up.”

## Fixing it produced another problem

  Computing from the total made reversals 0%. But with integer percentages, 1st and 2nd looking like the same % rose to around 30%. The top has titles with close totals. Rounding to integers erases the difference and they gather on the same number.

  So I changed the display to one decimal place (like 99.6%). Ties dropped to about 4%. It does not reach 0% because sometimes the totals really differ by less than 0.1%.

## Weak points of this measurement

- The respondents are synthetic. Real people answer differently.

- “Old” is a reconstruction: today’s ordering with the old display method applied. I did not run the code of that time. At the time, ratings and taste boosts had no cap, and the results may have differed.

- What I measured is only “does the display agree with the ranking,” not “is the ranking right for that person.”

## What I learned

> Make the number you show from the same yardstick you used to sort.
  It sounds obvious, but as calculations were added, only the order changed and the displayed number was left behind. Another point: rounding can erase a difference in rank. Where differences are small, just adding one digit brings back the visible order.

  The numbers in this article were measured on October 8, 2026 with 1,000 synthetic respondents (random numbers fixed). The commit record of that time is September 25, 2026.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/match-percent/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/shindan12/

# What changes when an anime quiz goes from 50 questions to 12?

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/shindan12/)

  Development log of the Anime Type Diagnosis / October 2026

  The Hardcore Anime Type Diagnosis (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/) has 50 questions in total. People said it was long, so I made it possible to get a result from just the first 12 questions. The remaining 38 are for those who want to answer them.

  But the result must change a bit by being shorter. I wanted to know how much with numbers, not feelings.

## How the 12 were chosen

  The quiz measures taste on 6 axes (worldview, aftertaste, structure, subtaste, visuals, viewing style). The 12-question version takes 2 questions from each axis, 12 in total. The calculation that produces the result is the same as with 50; unanswered questions are simply not counted.

  The 50 questions are 18 on the 6 axes, 2 on image quality and era, and 30 on taste elements (romance, horror, robots and so on). The 12-question version does not ask the last two (era and taste elements), so they do not affect the ordering of titles.

## How I measured: 1,000 synthetic respondents

  I cannot quickly have real people answer both 12 and 50 questions. So I used synthetic respondents. I say this up front: the numbers below are not the results of real people.

- For each respondent, I draw a “true taste” as a random number from −1 to +1 for the 6 axes, era, and 30 taste elements.

- Each answer is that “true taste” plus noise, rounded to 5 levels (leans A, slightly A, neither, slightly B, leans B).

- These answers are run through the same calculation as the real app (logic.js), once using only 12 questions and once using all 50.

  I do not know the size of the noise. People’s answers wobble even in the same mood, so I measured with three values: small (0.3), medium (0.5) and large (0.8). The titles used are the 6,074 with enough clues on the axes.

## The type mostly matches even with 12

  First, whether the type code (6 letters) is the same with 12 and 50 questions.

    Answer noise | All 6 letters match | Match per letter

    Small (0.3) | 75.6% | 94.7 to 96.1%

    Medium (0.5) | 60.8% | 90.9 to 93.7%

    Large (0.8) | 43.2% | 85.5 to 87.6%

  Looking letter by letter, even with medium noise more than 90% fall on the same side. Matching all 6 letters gets harder because you have to be right six times in a row. Even with 90% per letter, six in a row is a little over half.

## The single “title of fate” changes a lot

  Next, the “title of fate” the quiz shows at the end. It is one pick out of 6,074 titles, so the situation is different.

    Answer noise | Same single title | Any of the top 3 in common

    Small (0.3) | 21.7% | 63.4%

    Medium (0.5) | 15.7% | 52.7%

    Large (0.8) | 12.4% | 39.9%

  The title shown with 12 questions comes first with 50 questions for about 1 person in 5 to 8. With medium noise, about half have something in common in the top 3.

## At which stage does it change?

  I checked whether the reason is only “the 30 taste-element questions.” Between 12 and 50, I inserted 18 questions on the 6 axes only (no taste elements or era) and compared the single title (medium noise, 600 respondents).

    Compared | Same single title

    12 and 18 (axes only) | 33.8%

    18 and 50 | 27.5%

    12 and 50 | 15.0%

  Even just adding 6 axis questions before adding taste elements changes the single title for 2 in 3 people. When choosing one out of 6,000, a small difference in input reshuffles the order. It was not that “taste elements are doing harm.”

## Is 50 questions really closer to the right answer?

  In this setup I know the “true taste,” so the one title chosen from it can be treated as the correct answer. Do 12 and 50 get closer to it (medium noise)?

     | Same as the correct title | In the correct top 3

    12 questions | 8.2% | 14.9%

    50 questions | 14.3% | 28.5%

  50 questions is about 1.7 to 1.9 times closer to the correct answer. With small noise, the difference is 17.9% to 29.0% (single title) and 29.0% to 52.6% (top 3). The remaining 38 questions were not wasted. But even with 50, hitting the exact single title is a little over one in ten.

## Weak points of this measurement

- The respondents are synthetic. Real people’s tastes are not scattered like random numbers, and they are noisy in different ways.

- The noise size is a placeholder. That is why I measured with three values; I do not know the true one.

- The “correct answer” is correct on the quiz’s own yardstick. Whether it is something a person would really love is not measured.

- What I measured is “is it the same,” not “is it fun.”

## What I learned

> The type is set even when short. The single title of fate wobbles each time you add questions.
  The current design of giving a result at 12 questions and making the rest optional does not contradict these numbers. If you only want to know your type, 12 questions are enough, and only those who want a more accurate single title need continue. I think the result screen should say it that way.

  What I really want to check is real people’s answers: showing the same person the 12-question and the 50-question result and asking which feels right. If I get that far, I will write it in the next record.

  The measuring script is in the quiz’s repository (random numbers are fixed, so the same numbers can be reproduced).

  Take the quiz (https://koshinstudio.com/app/shindananime/en/)About the quiz (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/)

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/shindan12/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)


---

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/result-screen/

# The streaming buttons were shown even for titles you could not watch: making the quiz result screen true

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/result-screen/)

  Development log of the Anime Type Diagnosis / October 2026

  The result screen of the Hardcore Anime Type Diagnosis (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/) shows the cover of your title of fate and “where to watch” buttons. When I first built it, both the buttons and the images showed things that differed from reality. I recounted with my own data how large the difference was, and I am writing it down.

## The streaming buttons were the same two for every title

  In the first version, the streaming buttons on the result screen were only DMM TV and U-NEXT, the same two for any title. Pressing a button goes to that service’s search page. But the title is not necessarily available there.

  The quiz data includes, for each title, “which services stream it” (Filmarks streaming information). Of 6,091 titles, 4,489 (73.7%) have this. Counting whether the two buttons of that time really pointed to a place where you can watch, for these 4,489:

    The two buttons of that time | Titles | Share

    Both point to a place you can watch | 3,192 | 71.1%

    At least one points to a place you cannot watch | 1,297 | 28.9%

      of which both are places you cannot watch | 295 | 6.6%

  For one title in three or four, pressing the button did not find the title. It ended in “page not found.”

## The fix: narrow by real availability

- I increased the services from 2 to 12 (Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, U-NEXT, Hulu, DMM TV, ABEMA, d Anime Store, FOD, TELASA, Lemino, Bandai Channel). I opened the search URLs in a browser to check them.

- Buttons are made only for services in that title’s availability.

- But showing all of them would stretch the result card too tall. I sort by major services first (priority Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, U-NEXT, Hulu) and show only the top 3.

- For titles with unknown availability (the remaining 26.3%), there is no way to check, so I show the top 3 by popularity as before.

  Along the way I noticed that DMM TV’s search URL returned 404 (I changed /vod/search/ to /vod/list/).

  Availability is as of the time the data was collected. Streaming changes, so a title may not still be there when you press the button.

## The same thing was happening with images

  Some cover images were wrong or did not appear.

- http images do not appear. The quiz is served over https. If an image URL is http://, the browser blocks it as mixed content. (One official site had no certificate at all.) I treat http images as “none” and fill from an https image that comes later.

- Placeholder pictures were shown as real. “No image” placeholders and generic images shared by an official site are not the actual art. I now reject them.

- Logos got mixed in. Filmarks’ sharing image is a 240×240 square, and if the poster is not square, the company’s logo is put in the margin. I changed it to prefer another image embedded in the page (260×364, kept in the poster ratio). After re-fetching all 7,247 entries, the number using a poster-ratio image rose to 4,477 (89 are still in the old shape).

- No image at all. Most of the cause was that Annict and Filmarks split titles differently, so matching titles failed. By filling from images of the same series, the share with an image went from 77% to 86%.

  In the end, 92.5% of the 6,091 titles used by the quiz have an image.

## What I learned

> On a result screen, trust is decided less by looks than by “what happens when I press it.”

- Showing the same thing to everyone is easy, but wrong nearly 3 times in 10. Look at the real situation (availability) and narrow.

- Decide what to show when you “don’t know.” For the 26.3% with unknown availability, I fell back to the normal top 3.

- Reject what is not the real thing. Placeholders, generic images and images with a logo are worse than a blank, I decided.

  The shares in this article were counted on the quiz data (6,091 titles) as of October 8, 2026. The image counts come from the commit record (September 25, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/result-screen/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)


---

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/first-visit/

# Cutting six buttons to one: first-time players did not know what to press

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/first-visit/)

  Development log of Sushi Stack / October 2026

  The title screen of Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/) had six things you could press. Someone opening it for the first time did not know which to press. For the game portal launch, I narrowed “what a first-time player presses first” to one. I also wrote down, from my commits, two problems I fixed at the same time: saves vanishing, and what happens when you leave the screen.

## What a portal measures you by

  According to the commit, the portal I decided to submit to (CrazyGames) first has a trial stage (Basic Launch) shown to a limited audience for two weeks. Whether you move up to the next stage (Full Launch) is decided by these three things during that time.

- The share of people who start playing

- Average time played

- The share of people who come back

  Ads are disabled during this trial, so these are all that matters now. In other words, I had to improve two things by design: “people who open it start playing” and “they come back.”

## I narrowed it to one thing to press

  The title had six: Play, Menu, Ranking, Encyclopedia, Words and Info. To a first-timer, they all look equally heavy. So I rearranged it:

- One large “Play.”

- “Menu” as a thin second option.

- Ranking, Encyclopedia, Words and Info are folded into a thin row below.

  The ranking and the encyclopedia are “reasons to come back,” but they are not the first step the first time. That was my judgment.

## From the second visit, show that there is more

  The title shows the high score and how much of the encyclopedia is filled. But not to first-timers, because showing 0 points and 0 kinds means nothing.

## Inside the portal, saves vanish

  The portal runs the game in an iframe on a different domain. In some browsers, saving to the device (localStorage) is blocked inside it, and high scores and the encyclopedia vanish every time.

  If the portal provides a storage shelf (CrazyGames’ Data Module), I save there; if not, I keep it on the device as before. The portal’s part arrives later, so it keeps looking until it is found.

  The way I verified it was to plug in a fake storage shelf. When the shelf exists, it writes there and not to the device. Even in an environment where saving to the device throws an error, it starts and can be played.

## Leave the screen and it stops

  Until then, when you moved to another tab, only the deadline kept advancing, and it was already over when you came back. Now, when sent to the background, it pauses and the sound stops too. I actually fired the event for the screen being hidden (visibilitychange) and confirmed that it stops, that the score does not move after 1.5 seconds, and that it resumes.

## What I verified

- In all 14 languages, it fits on an iPhone SE screen.

- Across 7 screens × 3 languages, the 9:16 aspect ratio does not break.

- Two full playthroughs (163 moves in Japanese, 263 in English) at 60 fps with 0 errors.

## What I learned

> What a first-timer needs is not choices but a first step.

- “A reason to come back” and “the first step” are different things. The ranking and the encyclopedia have value, but they are not what a first-timer presses first.

- Saving may be unavailable depending on where it runs. That it worked on my machine does not guarantee it works inside a frame.

- Design what happens when someone leaves the screen. It is easy to build assuming people are watching all the time.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 7, 2026). The portal’s review conditions are as stated in the commit. After this, the game was rejected in review (Rejected by CrazyGames (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/crazygames/)).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/first-visit/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)


---

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/sushi-measure/

# “The pile settles at 89%” was wrong: my measurement was what was wrong

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/sushi-measure/)

  Development log of Sushi Stack / October 2026

  Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/) is a falling-block puzzle where you bump the same toppings together to merge them and grow them until the tub is full. While adjusting balance, I realized my own measurement result had been wrong. What was wrong, how I found it, and how I fixed it are written with the numbers in my commits.

  The numbers in this article are as of September 7, 2026. After this, the sizes of the pieces were scaled by 0.8 across the board, and changed again on September 10 (the kinds of falling pieces and the shape of the tub) (written in the conger eel article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anago/), in Japanese). They differ from today’s numbers.

## “It settles at 89%” was wrong

  My first measurement said “the pile settles at 89% of the tub’s height.” That would mean you can stack without overflowing and never lose.

  When I measured again, this was an illusion from counting the falling piece. The real pile kept rising. But it rose so slowly that even after dropping 240 pieces, only a third of the tub was filled. “A game you cannot lose” did not mean safe. It meant the pile does not grow enough to lose.

## Three causes

  The commit splits the causes into three. Each was confirmed by measurement before I removed it.

### 1. The size ladder went backward in three places

  When I lined up the sizes by the radius of a circle of the same area (equivalent radius), in three places the merged piece was smaller than the one before.

- Tamago was smaller than shari

- Otoro was smaller than uni

- Anago was smaller than otoro

  Merging produced a smaller piece than before. On the busiest path, “shari → tamago,” more than half of what I dropped vanished on the spot. So I rebuilt it as a monotonically increasing ladder with a size ratio of 1.19.

### 2. The pieces were too small for the tub

  I had used the 9:16 portrait tub directly as the drop area, so it was a vertical pit rather than a real sushi tub. I made the tub shallow enough to fit in the lower half of the screen, and drew a noren curtain (with the game name) and a plank wall in the empty space above. The deadline (past it, you lose) became the rim of the tub itself.

### 3. Big pieces fell through the floor

  The physical thickness of the walls and floor was only 12, the same as how it looked, so heavier pieces tunneled through the single plank and fell out of the tub. I made the thickness 80, and also rounded the position for pieces born from a merge that sink into a wall. I also added a cleanup for spilled pieces (sweepStrays).

## The numbers after the fix

    What I measured | Before | After

    How full the tub is after dropping 240 | about a third | —

    Drops until game over | not reached | 385 (rank: journeyman)

    Score (same conditions) | 7,298 | 10,658

  The pile moves up and down in front of the rim and opens up at once with a big merge. The tension this kind of game should have appeared. The score rose because the pieces that had been falling through and vanishing came back. I verified that 9:16 holds from iPhone SE to 15 Pro Max, in landscape and on desktop, that there is no overflow or errors, and that 60 fps holds with a full tub.

## What I learned

> What you measure is not necessarily what you want to know.
  The first “89%” counted the falling piece, so it was not measuring “the height of the pile.” I want to record that when a measurement looks too good, it is better to doubt what is being counted than the number itself. After the fix, I measured the numbers again with the same method as the conger eel article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anago/) (hundreds of auto-played games).

  The numbers in this article come from my commit record (September 7, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/sushi-measure/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)


---

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/anago/

# The conger eel was too big: finding why a merge puzzle’s last piece was out of reach

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anago/)

  Development log of Sushi Stack / September 2026

  Added on October 8, 2026. The numbers in this article are from the September 8 version. On September 10 I changed the sizes and the falling pieces once more (see “Afterward” at the bottom).

  After finishing Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/works/sushitsumu/), one thing bothered me: I could never reach the last piece, the golden sushi tub.

  However many times I played, I rarely even saw the spiny lobster before it. My feeling was “the conger eel is too big.” But if you tweak sizes by feel, something else usually breaks. I decided to measure first.

## Building a way to measure

  The game is a single HTML file, and time is driven by requestAnimationFrame. As it is, a game takes minutes, so I swapped in my own clock. I intercept requestAnimationFrame and setTimeout and advance them at any speed I like. If I also empty the drawing code, a game finishes in about 2 seconds.

  After that I wrote a bot of modest skill — merge first, and wait until the pile settles before placing — and let it run.

## What a hundred games showed

  First, a hundred games as it was.

  score   min 12,337 / median 21,664 / max 44,622
best piece reached   otoro 43 games  anago 52  spiny lobster 4  golden tub 0
  Zero for the golden tub. So where does it get stuck? Lining up the yield for moving up one tier (the share of times two of the lower piece became one of the next) made it clear.

    Merge | Yield

    Salmon → tuna | 94.0%

    Tuna → ikura gunkan | 91.9%

    Ikura gunkan → uni gunkan | 86.9%

    Uni gunkan → otoro | 71.4%

    Otoro → anago | 55.2%

    Anago → spiny lobster | 13.1%

    Spiny lobster → golden tub | 0.0%

  It falls gently and then there is a cliff at the anago. Of the 61 anago made, 53 (87%) were still sitting on the final board. Only 8 made it to a merge.

## The conger eel really was off

  Lining up the dimensions made it obvious at a glance. The inner width of the tub is 336.

    Piece | Width | Height | Width / inner | Growth from previous

    Otoro | 149 | 83 | 44% | ×1.34

    Anago | 247 | 71 | 74% | ×1.66

    Spiny lobster | 230 | 107 | 68% | ×0.93

    Golden tub | 210 | 210 | 62% | ×0.91

  The anago was the widest piece in the game. Wider than the spiny lobster after it, and wider than the final golden tub. Its width growth is 1.66 where other tiers are 1.0 to 1.34.

  As a result, when one anago lies down, the gap left beside it is 336 − 247 = 89. Only up to salmon (width 85) fits there; neither uni nor otoro. The anago spanned the tub and blocked the road ahead.

  By the way, the ladder of areas was clean. Every tier was a constant “0.70 to 0.71 times the two pieces below.” Only the order of widths was broken.

## Fix it, but measure first

  I made only the width 4/5 (247 → 198) and ran another hundred games.

     | Median | Max | Anago | Spiny lobster | Anago → lobster yield

    247 × 71 (original) | 21,664 | 44,622 | 61 | 4 | 13.1%

    198 × 71 | 24,858 | 47,392 | 79 | 12 | 30.4%

    205 × 85 (keep the area) | 25,149 | 36,350 | 33 | 1 | 6.1%

  The third row was interesting. The version that got thinner while keeping its area made the late game not move at all. What mattered was not “thin” itself but that the anago no longer spanned the tub and big pieces could sit beside it.

## Still, the golden tub is out of reach

  Spiny lobsters appeared three times as often. But the golden tub was still zero. Here another wall showed up.

  The falling pieces were only three kinds: shari, tamago and shrimp. After subtracting gari, each drop is only 2.217 shari-equivalents. Meanwhile:

    To make | In shari | Drops needed with zero waste

    1 anago | 256 | 115

    1 spiny lobster | 512 | 231

    1 golden tub | 1,024 | 462

  The measured number of drops was a median of 280 and 426 at most. Even with zero waste, there were not enough moves. 231 drops for a spiny lobster is right at the border, which matches the measured 12 in a hundred.

## The real cause: the sushi was too big

  In Suika Game some people make “twin watermelons.” That works because the last fruit is small enough compared with the box. What about mine?

  With one golden tub in place, I must make a second spiny lobster
  golden tub 210 + lobster 107 + lobster 107 = 424px  >  usable height 302px
  side by side: lobster 230 × 2 = 460px               >  inner width 336px
  It fits neither vertically nor horizontally. This is not a matter of luck or skill: there is no gap for it to fit in.

  So I tried scaling all the pieces by 0.8 across the board. The diameter of the golden tub goes from 210 to 168, exactly half of the tub’s inner width of 336.

     | Median | Max | Reach golden tub | Reach lobster | One game

    Original size | 24,858 | 47,392 | 0 / 100 games | 12% | 3.7 min

    0.8x | 58,741 | 103,630 | 7% | 65% | 7.7 min

  At last the road was open. The spiny lobster is reached nearly every game, and the golden tub appears once in a dozen or so. The twin never appeared in sixty games, which is not a failure; it is probably the right state. It became a legend within reach.

## I redrew the ranks too

  Scores came out 2.4 times higher, so I had to redo all the rank thresholds. For the top rank, matching the fact that games reaching the golden tub all scored 86,000 or more, I set 85,000. The number is the same as before but its meaning changed. Before, it was a decoration nobody could reach; now it is “make the golden tub and you are a legend.”

## I measured again after release

  With the fixed version, using the same contents as what is published, I ran three hundred games again. The shape I saw at 100 games continues.

    Measured | 300 games

    Median score | 59,305

    Highest score | 163,426

    Reached grilled anago | 99%

    Reached spiny lobster | 73%

    Reached golden sushi tub | 10% (31 games)

    Two golden tubs in one game | 0

    Length of one game (median) | 7.7 min

    Pieces placed (median) | 589

    Longest chain | 10

  The bot is tools/sim/bot.js. It merges first and waits for the pile to settle before placing. A human can play better or worse, but it was enough to compare before and after with the same yardstick.

## What I learned

> My feeling was right. But the cause was not where I thought.
  The feeling that “the anago is too big” was correct. But thinning only the anago did not move the late game, and the real cause was that all of the sushi was too big for the tub. If I had suspected and fixed one place, I probably would never have gotten there.

  Collecting statistics from three hundred games took about ten minutes in total. It was much faster and more reliable than tweaking by feel three times and checking.

## Afterward (September 10): I changed it again

  After this article, I submitted the game to CrazyGames and was rejected (details in another article (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/crazygames/)). What I reconsidered was that tension in the tub did not happen even once in the few minutes of review. The commit says: measured with auto-play, one game is a median of 594 moves, 7.5 minutes. 30 minutes for a human. The tub never fills, and dangerous moments never come.

  I left each tier’s dimensions and area ratios alone and changed only places where I could fix without losing the feeling of “growing as you merge.” I chose them by measuring with auto-play.

- Falling pieces from 3 kinds to 5. I added salmon and tuna to shari, tamago and shrimp (weights 1:1:2:3:2). More piles up per move and the median went from 594 to 279 moves. The rate of reaching higher tiers also went up.

- The shape of the tub. Rim from 320 to 250, height from 308 to 378. The play area went from 45% to 62% of the screen.

- Spiny lobster and golden tub scaled another 0.89x. The area ratio from anago to spiny lobster alone had jumped to 1.76 and is now 1.40, in line. The leftover when two golden tubs sit side by side went from 0 px to 36 px, and a double golden tub (golden tubs merging) became possible in real play. The logic had been there before but never happened once in 300 games.

  With a game half as long, scores also fell by about 20% (auto-play median from 59,305 to 46,529). I re-took the rank thresholds from quantiles of 60 games and restored the same distribution as before (apprentice 7%, journeyman 28%, head chef 40%, master 17%, legend 8%). I also raised the double-golden-tub reward from 8,000 to 25,000, because merges up to making one golden tub already give about 34,000 points.

  The moves needed for a double golden tub are 275 even with zero waste. Auto-play makes one golden tub in about 2.0 times the ideal, so auto-play cannot reach it (0 in 40 games). It is set up so that only a person who tidies the pile and plays well can reach it.

  The numbers in the “0.8x” table above (median 58,741, 7.7 minutes a game and so on) are from the September 8 version. They differ from the current numbers.

  Related

  Play (https://koshinstudio.com/play/sushitsumu/)

# A typo born once multiplied across shops: the “30th SEREBRATION” incident

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/typo-catalog/)

  Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  In my iOS app Torecadash, a user reported: “this article duplicates another one, and the product name is odd.” When I looked, a misspelled product created just once was being reused every time an article from a shop arrived, and it kept multiplying. The cause, the fix, and the limits of the fix are written from my commit record.

  This is a development log of the app.

## What was reported

  Articles for the Pokémon Card product “30th CELEBRATION” were appearing at several shops under the product name “30th SEREBRATION” (a misspelling of CELEBRATION). They also duplicated the articles with the correct name for the same product.

## Root cause: a short heading did not match the official name

  Summaries posted by roundup sites have short headings like “‘30th CELEBRATION’.” The official name in the app’s catalog is “Expansion Pack ‘30th CELEBRATION’.” The short heading is shorter than the official name, so a one-direction check of “does the article title contain the official name” did not match.

  When there was no match, it went to AI matching. Along that path, just once, a misspelled product “30th SEREBRATION” was created. My commit guesses it came from a mistake when converting another spelling in the catalog (“30th セレブレーション” in katakana) to the Latin alphabet.

  The real trouble came next. Once a misspelled product is created, it is reused repeatedly as an “existing product.” Each time a new article arrived from a shop, the same typo and the same duplicate were mass-produced.

## First, fix the data

  I checked all shops. At three shops including Bic Camera, Sanyodo Shoten and Game Plaza, it duplicated an article with the correct name, so I hid one of each. The other 10 articles only needed their product reassigned. 13 articles in total. I deleted the misspelled product.

  I left one thing alone on purpose. The existing tool for merging products judged “SEREBRATION” and “CELEBRATION” as different products and refused. That gate is intentionally strict, so I did not loosen it. I fixed these by hand, one by one.

## The real prevention: pick up short headings by “exact match”

  Fixing the data alone would let it happen again. So I fixed the matching with the official catalog. I strip one generic form word (such as “Expansion Pack”) from the front of the official name, and treat it as the same product only when what remains exactly matches the article title.

  I chose “exact match” instead of “contains” so as not to pick up more specific, different products such as “30th CELEBRATION Card Set X.” Now it matches the official catalog correctly from the start, and never reaches the AI matching path where the typo was born. The results I confirmed:

- “30th CELEBRATION” matches the official product correctly.

- The misspelled “30th SEREBRATION” does not match (it is not wrongly treated as official).

- Existing exact matches, other genres and unrelated set names behave as before.

## Safety net: an edit-distance check, and its limits

  As a precaution, I also added a check at the point just before a product is created: “a candidate with a small edit distance from the official catalog is strongly suspected to be a typo, so reject it.” But this check alone cannot catch “30th SEREBRATION” against “Expansion Pack ‘30th CELEBRATION’.” The difference in length is too large, so the edit distance is far (I confirmed this).

  So the safety net does not work for this case. What works is the main fix above. I kept the safety net to catch other typos of the same length (for example, Weiss Schwarz names missing a “/”). I also built a read-only audit that finds catalog entries suspected of typos. At the time of the commit it found 21 suspects of the same shape.

## What I learned

> A mistake born once becomes “existing,” and multiplies.

- Wrong data multiplies by itself. What was created becomes the thing reused next time. Fixing the data is not enough; you have to fix the path by which it is born.

- “Exact match” over “contains.” Picking up widely drags in other products.

- Check the limits of a safety net and write them down. Instead of assuming “this check prevents it,” I checked first that it does not work for this typo.

- Do not loosen a strict gate. What the merge tool rejected was the correct behavior.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 28, 2026). How the typo was born is the commit’s guess.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/typo-catalog/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# The “9-pack set” was nine different products: the same product that never matched

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-9set/)

  Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  My iOS app Torecadash collects lottery and first-come sale information for trading cards and notifies users. To check for gaps, I match and count listings on other roundup sites (Chusen Zukan, Pokechu) against the articles in my own app. When I measured on October 7, most gaps came from a small discrepancy: the same product that never matched. This is from my hand-over notes and commit record.

  This is a development log of the app.

## What I measured

  With read-only access, I checked “are all lotteries introduced by the roundup sites shown in the app?”

- Chusen Zukan: of 90 open lotteries, 49 (54%) were displayed in the app. 12 had an article but were hidden, and 29 were not in the feed.

- Pokechu: 18 of 21 (86%).

- X roundup posts: 606 posts in 72 hours. Only 9 linked to an article.

## Of the 12 hidden, 7 were because the row was wrong

  Looking at the 12 hidden, in 7 the roundup site’s row named a different product from the application page. Four shops of one chain said “energy card set,” and three others said “expansion pack.” The application page (the lottery form) and the shop’s X account showed it was actually a “card set, 9-pack set, 10,800 yen.”

  The app’s “price gate” (which rejects items whose listing price does not match the product’s list price) was correctly rejecting them. What was wrong was not the gate but the product mix-up. I reassigned the products and restored them to visible.

## What the “9-pack set” really was

  This “9-pack set” is a card set of Pokémon Card 30th CELEBRATION, which is 9 products, each a set of the starter trio from nine generations. The catalog had these 9 products registered correctly from the beginning. But each time a marketplace listing or X monitoring created a new article, a bug registered it as another product named after only one of the three, in several of the 9 products. For example, a product with only “Hinoarashi.”

## The same product, never matching

  The matching has a process that makes a “key” for comparing product names. It had a left-right asymmetry.

- On the other side, “card set 9-pack” has the trailing “9-pack” dropped before comparing.

- On the catalog side, “card set 9-kinds set” is not dropped.

  The same product never matched. As a result, the other side’s name was wrongly resolved to a different product such as “energy card set” or “expansion pack.” That was where the mix-up came from. I applied the same rule to both sides (drop “N packs,” “N kinds” and “set”), and also made names that carry a number specification not be settled to one by partial match. I confirmed that there are 0 key collisions across the whole catalog.

## Another hole: the previous article blocked the next round

  The main cause of “not in the feed” was elsewhere. The article ID was made from “roundup URL + shop + product,” and it did not include the lottery round. The expired article from the previous round stopped the new round’s article for the same shop and product from being created (“the same article ID already exists”). If the new round’s deadline is more than 1 day later than the previous one, it now creates an article with a different ID that adds the date.

## Result

    Coverage | Before | After

    Chusen Zukan (90 open) | 54% (49) | 91% (82)

    Pokechu | 86% | 90%

  The remainder are cases where the application page only says “various products” so the product cannot be identified, where the page has no clue to the shop name, and so on. They include ones I decided not to adopt for safety. The misses did not become zero.

## What I learned

> A gate that rejected correctly and wrong data are different problems.

- Before doubting what was rejected, look at why it was rejected. The price gate worked correctly; what was wrong was the product mix-up.

- The cause of “does not match” can be a left-right asymmetry in how you compare. The same product never matching was a mismatch of rules, not dirty data.

- You do not see gaps unless you count coverage. Only when the number 54% came out did I know where to fix.

  The numbers in this article come from my hand-over notes (§272, §281) and commit record (October 7, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-9set/).

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Splitting a “9-pack set” by contents created 80 fake products

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/fake-products/)

  Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  While inspecting the product list of my iOS app Torecadash, I found 80 products that do not exist around the Pokémon Card “30th CELEBRATION Card Set.” There are only 9 official products. The other 80 were fake products created as a result of splitting a “9-pack set” by its contents. What happened and how I fixed it are written from my hand-over notes.

  This is a development log of the app.

## The 9-pack set was “one product”

  The lottery for a “card set (9-pack set)” that a shop offers is one product. In the catalog it is registered as a “9-kinds set” (10,800 yen). But the app’s product matching (the step that splits an article mentioning several products into one per product) split this title by contents. Names of the nine contents, such as “Mega Mewtwo X” and “Nyabby,” were each treated as a separate product.

  As a result, this is what it looked like:

    State | Count

    Original articles that had been split (parents) were hidden | 22

    Articles created by splitting (children) | 190 (63 visible)

    Fake products created for the children | 80

  On screen, one lottery appeared as if it were separate lotteries for each content item.

## The fix: stop the entry, then put things back

- Do not split at the entry. A title of the form “card set” + “N kinds” is not split.

- Restore the parents. I put the 22 hidden parents back onto the “9-kinds set” product. How I restored each differed (5 back to visible, 3 treated as duplicates because the same shop already had a visible 9-pack set, 13 whose deadline had passed, and 1 with no deadline).

- Detach the children. I marked the 190 children with a “wrong split” flag (hiddenByWrongSplit), hid them, and removed their link to a product.

- Delete the fake products. I deleted the 80. Before deleting, I confirmed that nothing referenced them and saved the original contents as a backup.

  There is an exception. A listing like “Starter Set ex Nyaoha / Hogator / Quaxly 3-kinds set,” where the title spells out all the product names, is still split as before. What I learned this time is that an “N-kinds set” is sold as one product.

## Other fake products found in the same inspection

- Things that are not cards. Products for apparel, figures, tournaments and music CDs had been created between September 3 and October 3. I added a gate at the entry for names that are not cards (looksLikeNonCardMerchOrEventName) and confirmed 0 false hits across the whole catalog. I deleted 25.

- Single cards. I deleted a total of 30 single-card products that came from Snkrdunk listings. Some of those single cards had a “list price.” Having a list price turned out not to be proof of an official cross-check. The proof is imageIsOfficial.

- A product combining three packs. I deleted one unofficial product that lined up several set names. Its 49 linked articles were all expired.

  To watch for these, I added an audit (audit_catalog_clean.js). Each time it counts five things: single-card products, products with several set names, mismatches between an application page’s title and the product, drift of list prices copied from products, and products with non-card names.

## What I learned

> A “split” process needs a “do not split” condition.

- Splitting one product into several multiplies fake products. Splitting should happen only after checking “is it really several products.”

- Count references before deleting. I deleted only after confirming zero references and a saved backup.

- Stop fake products at both the entry and the contents. An entry gate alone leaves what already exists. An audit counts what remains.

  This article is written from my hand-over notes (§272) (October 7, 2026). The counts are as written in the notes.

  Related

- The “9-pack set” was nine different products (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/torecadash-9set/) — the matching record for the same product

- I counted duplicates as zero, but the audit found 112 pairs (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/dup-zero/) — another record from the same day

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/fake-products/).

# Measuring Qiita’s “posting too frequently” limit: a new account could not create another article for about 30 minutes

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/qiita-post-interval/)

  This site / October 2026

  I published summaries of this site’s articles on Qiita. But when I tried to create a second one right after the first, the new-article screen would not open and said “posting too frequently.” How long you have to wait did not seem to be written officially, so I measured it.

  I measured only this one new account (registered on October 8, 2026). This does not mean it is a general specification of Qiita.

## How I measured

- I record the time an article was published (for the first one, “14:19” from Qiita’s notification, which is only to the minute).

- Then about every 5 minutes, I open the “new article” screen in a logged-in browser. If it opens it is “allowed”; if I am redirected to the trend page it is “blocked.” I record this with the time.

- When it opens, I publish the next article right away and take the same record again.

- I did not do anything like slipping past the limit by posting. I only checked whether the screen opens.

## Results

    Interval | Previous article published at | Last blocked check | First allowed check | Publish until it opens

    1st → 2nd | 14:19 | 14:46:34 (blocked) | 14:51:50 (allowed) | about 27.6 to 32.8 min

    2nd → 3rd | 14:52:36 | 15:19:03 (blocked) | 15:24:18 (allowed) | about 26.5 to 31.7 min

    3rd → 4th | 15:24:59 | 15:30:29 (blocked) | 16:10:02 (allowed) | 5.5 to 45.1 min (unknown)

- The first and second were both around 30 minutes. The range exists because I only checked every 5 minutes. “It opened” somewhere between the last block and the first allow.

- The third is unusable data. The next check after 15:30:29 is not in the record until 16:10:02. The checks were not running for about 40 minutes (I have not confirmed why; the computer may have been asleep). The opening time is somewhere in there, and the interval is unknown.

- The wording “posting too frequently” could not be captured by the automatic check (I was only sent back to the trend page, and no message appeared). It is the wording I saw on my own screen.

## What I know and what I do not

> On this new account, I could not create the next article for about 30 minutes after publishing.

- Two measurements agreed at about 30 minutes. But it is only two. It is not a number that lets me say “exactly 30 minutes.”

- A personal blog from 2018 reported “you cannot post or edit for about 30 minutes after posting.” It is close to this measurement. But it is another person’s report from another time, and I do not know whether it is the same mechanism.

- I do not know whether it is a limit only for newly registered accounts or applies to ordinary ones too. I measured only one account.

- I also do not know whether the limit changes with the number of posts (from which post it gets longer), because the third was lost.

## Reflections on the measurement

- The check interval was 5 minutes. A 5-minute range was left each time. Checking every minute would shrink it.

- I did not notice that the checks had stopped. I needed a mechanism to warn me when there is no check record for a set time.

- The first publish time was only to the minute. I could take seconds only from the second onward, where I recorded the time myself.

## What I could not confirm

- Qiita’s official rule on posting interval (I looked, but found no public description).

- The interval for the third (the record is missing).

- The same measurement on other accounts.

- Whether the limit changes with the age of the account or the number of posts.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/qiita-post-interval/).

# Rejected by CrazyGames with no reason given: I recorded the game and found four problems

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/crazygames/)

  Development log of Sushi Stack / October 2026

  I submitted Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/), my merge puzzle game, to the browser-game portal CrazyGames, and it was rejected. The only reason given was that “overall quality does not meet expectations.” So I captured the game myself and looked for the problem. I found four. This is written from my commit record.

## When no reason is given

  “Quality” does not tell me what is wrong. The commit notes say that once I actually recorded the game, I recognized the problems. A reviewer plays for a few minutes and judges from what is on the screen. So I decided to look at the same screen the reviewer saw.

## The four I found

### 1. A black line across the screen

  The darkening effect for the background left the edge where the wall meets the floor, so a black straight line ran across the screen and a vertical seam showed at the rim of the tub. It looked broken. I blended the boundary and changed the edge fade from a straight cut to a curve.

### 2. On a wide screen, the play area was only 30%

  On a wide screen the play area took 30% of the screen and the rest was just dark. I put the evolution chain (what merges into what) on the left. In a merge game it is the first thing players look for, and I had hidden it inside the encyclopedia.

### 3. The silhouettes of unlocked tiers were invisible

  Tiers not yet reached are shown as silhouettes. But I drew dark brown silhouettes on a dark background, so they could not be seen. I made it possible to pass a lighter silhouette.

### 4. Tension never happened

  The fourth was heavier than looks. Measured with auto-play, one game was a median of 594 moves, about 7.5 minutes, and my commit says “30 minutes for a human.” The tub never filled up, so the dangerous moments never came. In the few minutes a reviewer spends, tension never occurred even once.

## The fix: measure, then choose

  I decided not to touch the size or area ratio of each tier, since that would damage the feeling of merging into something bigger. I used auto-play to find places I could change without losing that feeling. I also gave my balance-testing tool a way to swap sizes and the spawn distribution from outside, and ran candidates in bulk to compare.

    What changed | Before | After

    Items that fall | 3 kinds | 5 kinds (added salmon and tuna)

    Moves per game (auto-play median) | 594 | 279

    Tub rim / height | 320 / 308 | 250 / 378

    Share of screen used by the play area | 45% | 62%

    Area ratio, conger eel to spiny lobster | 1.76 | 1.40

    Leftover width when two gold tubs sit side by side | 0 px | 36 px

  Now two gold tubs fit side by side, so a gold-tub merge (merging gold tubs together) works in real play. The logic had been there before, but it never happened once in 300 games. A game is half as long, so scores also dropped by about 20% (auto-play median from 59,305 to 46,529). I recalculated the ranking thresholds.

## What I learned

> “Low quality” was four separate problems.
  Two were about appearance, one about where information was placed, and one about the substance of play. When no reason is given, the first thing to do is look at the screen the other person saw. For someone who plays for a few minutes, tension that builds over 30 minutes does not exist.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 10, 2026). The result of a re-review is not included.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/crazygames/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Measuring the gap between ads in time, not in plays

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/adgap/)

  Development log of Sushi Stack / October 2026

  Sushi Stack has a mechanism that can insert one ad at the break between one game and the next. At first I set it to “one ad per 5 plays,” and the next day I changed it to count time, not plays. This is the reason and a record of how it behaves.

  This site does not show ads yet (the ad loader is left empty). This is about a mechanism I built ahead of time for when ads are turned on.

## The first rule: one ad per 5 plays

  In the first version on September 7, an ad was inserted before “one more game” every 5 plays, and never on the first play. The idea was to skip the first game to protect the first impression. The game detects which of CrazyGames, Poki or Google it runs on, uses that SDK if there is one, and passes through if there is none.

## Why it did not fit

  The next day, September 8, I dropped this counting. The commit gives two reasons.

- If one game is long, ads never appear. A game can last 30 minutes, so the 5th play comes 2.5 hours later. Almost nobody plays that long.

- If games end quickly, ads appear one after another. After several quick losses, several ads show up within minutes.

  Both come from counting plays. What bothers a player is not the number of ads but the time between ads. So I changed what I count to time.

## The rule after the change

- No ad on the first game (as before).

- For someone who has not seen an ad yet, one ad at the break after the second game.

- After that, only when at least 7 minutes have passed since the last ad, one ad at the next break.

  The time of the last ad is remembered in the browser (localStorage). Nothing is sent to a server. The behavior I checked:

    Situation | Ad

    First play | None

    Second play (no ad shown yet) | Shown

    1 minute / 6 minutes since the last ad | None

    8 minutes since the last ad | Shown

    After a long game (40 minutes) | Shown

  For the earlier version (one ad per 5 plays), I ran 7 games with a fake CrazyGames SDK and confirmed that “an ad appears once after the 5th game” and that “with no SDK, none appears and there are zero errors.” For the time-based version too, I checked that the screen always returns after an ad ends.

## What I noticed while writing

  How I chose “7 minutes” is not in the commit. I will be honest: the reason is not recorded.

  What bothers me most is the length of a game. The commit’s “a game can take 30 minutes” was later, in the September 10 commit, written as “median 7.5 minutes in auto-play, 30 minutes for a human.” So 30 minutes is a guess, not a measured number. The 7.5 minutes of auto-play (7.7 minutes in the conger eel article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anago/), in Japanese) is the measured one.

  And on September 10 a game became half as long, so the earlier table is out of date. Recalculating (I put an auto-play game at half of 7.7 minutes, about 3.8 minutes):

    Length of one game | One per 5 plays (old) | One per 7 minutes (new)

    About 3.8 min (auto-play, after halving) | One per about 19 min | About one per 2 games

    About 15 min (half of “30 for a human”) | One per about 75 min | Every game

  I still have not measured how long a game takes a person. Whether 7 minutes is long or short cannot be decided without that. Measuring the length of a game comes before turning ads on.

## What I learned

> Counting plays makes ad frequency swing with how people play. Counting time does not.
  But changing to time did not make the frequency right. My current conclusion is that whether 7 minutes is long or short cannot be decided until I know how long a game takes a person. When I am ready to turn ads on, I will measure that first.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/adgap/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/ascii-text/

# Japanese text garbled in the CrazyGames preview: the file was correct, the cause was never found, so I escaped to ASCII

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/ascii-text/)

  Development log of Sushi Stack / October 2026

  When I opened Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/) in a game portal’s preview, a report said that only the character 連 in “大連鎖！” (Big Chain!) appeared broken. I checked the file and the character was stored correctly. This is how I moved on, without knowing the cause, by making it a form that does not matter if it breaks, from my commit record.

## Only one character breaks

  The report came from the CrazyGames preview. When a chain happens in the game, “大連鎖！” appears on screen. That one character, 連, was rendered broken. The other characters were fine.

  I first checked the game file itself. The byte sequence was correct. So the file on my side was not broken. It had to break somewhere in the hand-off before it reached the portal, or somewhere in how the portal read it. The commit does not say where. I have not identified the cause.

## How to fix something whose cause you cannot find

  If the cause is outside my hands, I decided to make a form that does not matter wherever it breaks.

- Replace displayed text with ASCII-only notation. Do not write Japanese characters directly in the file. In scripts use \uXXXX, in HTML text and attributes use &#xXXXX;. Even if multi-byte characters get corrupted midway, ASCII has nothing to corrupt.

- Leave the replacement to a tool (tools/asciify.mjs). I write in Japanese, then run the tool. It gives the same result no matter how many times I run it. Comments stay in Japanese so they stay readable (they never appear on screen).

- Add a font that has the kanji to the end of the font stack. That also closes the path where a font lacks the character and it does not show.

## Two other problems found in the same check

- Emoji do not show on some devices. The globe and mobile-phone emoji are missing on some devices. I redrew them as SVG shapes.

- Floating text during a chain overlaps and cannot be read. Text that appears at nearby positions now moves upward to avoid overlap.

## The next day: do 14 languages fit in their boxes?

  The game supports 14 languages. Translations are often longer than the Japanese and overflow easily in the side column on PC (192 px wide) and inside cards. I added a tool that switches through the languages in turn and counts anything that sticks out of its parent box or scrolls sideways.

  The result: no overflow in 14 languages × 2 screen sizes. As with broken characters, “nothing overflows” is more reliable counted than eyeballed.

## What I learned

> When you do not know the cause, stop depending on the place where the cause is.

- A correct file does not mean a correct screen. The hand-off and the portal’s reading are things I cannot fix.

- Write down what you do not know. I still do not know why 連 broke. ASCII escaping did not fix the cause. It only made the game unaffected by it.

- Have a machine count visual breakage. Checking 14 languages by eye is not realistic.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 7 and 8, 2026). The cause of the broken character is not in the record, so it is not written here.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/ascii-text/).

# Works on my machine, breaks when deployed: four incidents shipping a static site to Cloudflare Pages

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/deploy-gotchas/)

  Development log of Koshin Studio / October 2026

  This site is assembled from HTML and deployed to Cloudflare Pages. In a single day in September, four incidents of the “works on my machine, breaks when deployed” kind followed one another. This is written in order, from my commit record.

## 1. I fixed it, but the old version kept running

  I fixed how the logo bursts, but returning visitors still saw the old motion. The cause was that the file names of style.css and motion.js did not change. A browser that had loaded them once held them for a day. My own screen was always fresh after a deploy, so I did not notice.

  The fix is to append a mark made from the file’s contents (the first 8 hex digits of its sha1) to the name, like style.css?v=19008d13. When the contents change, it is fetched as a different file. I added the same mark to the font. When I rebuilt the font with more characters and a browser held the old one, characters did not render (tofu boxes).

  Since names now change, I extended the cache lifetime from 1 day to 30 days. I checked that rebuilding does not add marks, and that the same contents give the same mark.

## 2. Contents multiplied every time I rebuilt

  On the Sushi Stack page, the breadcrumb list had grown to 14 items. The build of this site works by rewriting finished HTML. Before inserting, it “removes” the previous insertion. If the removing side does not match, things pile up on every build.

- Breadcrumbs: the removing regular expression only looked for class="crumbs" and did not match the real element, which had an aria-label.

- RSS link: there was no removing side at all, so it was added every time.

  I made a machine find incidents of the same shape. The main check is to build twice and report any page that differs by even one character. It also checks that the header band, footer, body, breadcrumbs and headings are not duplicated. Right after adding it, the RSS case was caught.

## 3. I had committed a symlink that points into my own environment

  tools/node_modules was a symbolic link pointing inside this environment. Once it was in git, other machines had no target for it, and counting files for the deploy (wrangler) stopped. It actually stopped. I removed it from tracking, and added a check that reports any symlink among tracked files.

## 4. It worked only on my machine

  My machine has images that are not in git, and leftovers from earlier builds. Because of those, things work only locally and give a 404 once deployed. The favicon of the play pages was exactly that.

  So I added a check that copies only the committed contents to another place, rebuilds there, and loads every page. Files I decided not to ship (those listed in .assetsignore) are dropped from the copy in the same way. In that run, 8 files were dropped and none was missing on the 12 pages.

## What I learned

> The least trustworthy thing is my own machine.

- A file whose name does not change never delivers its new contents. Put a mark of the contents in the name.

- Rebuild accidents are found by “do it twice, is it the same?” The first result always looks clean.

- What is on your machine and what you ship are different. Check from a fresh clone.

  I did not notice any of the four myself. They were found only after I added checks. Walking through the pages did not reveal them.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 8, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/deploy-gotchas/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)
